I've been playing Counter-Strike for well over 20,000 hours, and at this point, it's more than just a game for me. I've played through different eras of Counter-Strike and experienced both the highs and the lows. Despite all the changes, CS2 still delivers something that no other FPS has managed to replace for me.

The gunplay is incredibly satisfying, movement feels great, and the competitive nature of the game keeps me coming back day after day. There are matches that make you want to queue again immediately, and there are matches that make you question your sanity. That's Counter-Strike.

Of course, not everything is perfect. Cheaters remain one of the biggest frustrations in the game. Running into suspicious players can ruin the experience, especially in competitive matches, and I genuinely hope Valve continues to improve anti-cheat measures because the community deserves better. Nothing kills the excitement of a close match faster than feeling like you're playing against someone with an unfair advantage.

That being said, I still believe CS2 has the best core gameplay in the genre. No battle passes, no gimmicks, no hero abilities can replace the simple formula that has kept Counter-Strike alive for decades. Every round matters, every clutch feels rewarding, and every mistake teaches you something.

I've taken breaks from the game many times, tried countless other shooters, sold skins, bought skins again, and somehow I always find myself coming back. There is just something special about Counter-Strike that is difficult to explain unless you've spent thousands of hours with it.

After more than 20,000 hours, I can honestly say that I'm probably addicted at this point, but I don't regret a single minute. Even with the problems, even with the cheaters, this is still my favorite competitive game of all time.

Valve still has work to do, but the foundation is fantastic, and I believe the game will only continue to improve.

I grew up playing this franchise. It shaped my childhood, fueled my passion for gaming, and ultimately became my career. Transitioning from a kid playing for fun to competing as a professional player gives me a unique perspective on Counter-Strike 2.Valve had a massive task in replacing CS:GO, and while the transition hasn't been flawless, CS2 successfully modernizes the greatest tactical shooter of all time.The ProsStrategic Evolution: Volumetric smoke physics completely rewrite the tactical playbook. Displacing smoke with HE grenades adds incredible depth to professional play.Visual Clarity: The Source 2 engine provides vibrant lighting and vastly improved player visibility, which is crucial for high-level competitive integrity.Audio Engineering: Sound cues are sharper and more directional, allowing for precise, instinctual audio positioning.The ConsSubtick Consistency: From a professional standpoint, the subtick system still lacks the crisp, predictable responsiveness of legacy 128-tick servers.Performance Optimization: Higher hardware demands can cause occasional frame-rate drops, requiring a high-end PC to maintain stable tournament-level performance.Final VerdictCounter-Strike 2 honors the legacy of its predecessor while building the foundation for the future of esports. It preserves the unforgiving skill ceiling I fell in love with as a kid, while delivering the modern upgrades needed for the next decade of competition. Whether you are a casual player or a aspiring pro, this is still the pinnacle of tactical shooters.

The Source 2 transition brought reworked visuals and physics-based smokes that genuinely move the game forward; the smokes are so pretty now you almost want to get lost in them. The sub-tick system changed how shooting feels, and thanks to it I'm absolutely certain every death of mine is perfectly fair (it's not). Still, the movement and gunplay kept that classic bone structure, so veterans feel right at home immediately.
On the anti-cheat side, things are better than before now that VACnet has improved, but you'll still bump into the occasional "suspicious" people in Premier. To be honest, I also learned to check my own crosshair placement before blaming a cheater. Despite all that, the competitive depth, economy management, and team play are still the best in the genre.
That said, I genuinely miss CS:GO. There was something about its feel, its cleaner simplicity and that old-school identity, that CS2 hasn't fully recaptured for me. CS:GO was just better in a lot of ways, and a part of me wishes I could go back.
It's free, constantly updated, and has a massive community. You can spend hours trash-talking with your friends, what more could you want? It's a game every FPS fan should try.
Highly recommend, but consider this a warning so your life doesn't get derailed.

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) stands as the successor to one of the most iconic tactical shooters in gaming history. By transitioning from the aging CS:GO engine to Source 2, Valve aimed to modernize the experience while preserving the core competitive integrity that defined the series for over two decades.

---

### The Good: Refined Mechanics and Competitive Depth

* **Source 2 Engine:** The visual overhaul is significant. Lighting, textures, and particle effects are drastically improved, making the game look sharper and more immersive.
* **Dynamic Smoke Grenades:** This is arguably the most impactful gameplay change. Smokes are now volumetric objects that interact with the environment. They react to bullets and explosions, allowing players to clear lines of sight temporarily—a feature that adds an incredible layer of strategic depth.
* **Sub-Tick Architecture:** Valve introduced a new "sub-tick" update system intended to bridge the gap between high-tick rate servers and lower-tick environments. While controversial at launch, it fundamentally aims to make movement and shooting more responsive and consistent across all player tiers.
* **The Premier Mode:** The revamped matchmaking system offers a clear, ELO-based ranking path that feels more professional and rewarding than the traditional matchmaking ranks.

### The Fun: The "Culture" of CS

* **Skin Economy:** The digital economy surrounding CS2 is unmatched. Collecting, trading, and showcasing skins is a game in itself, often keeping players engaged even when they aren't actively grinding ranks.
* **The Community & Custom Servers:** From intense "Surf" maps and "KZ" (parkour) servers to casual community modes, the social aspect of jumping into a server with friends remains the heart of the experience.
* **The "Clutch" Moments:** There is no adrenaline rush quite like being the last player alive in a 1v3 situation, successfully defusing the bomb, and hearing the roar of your teammates. These high-stakes moments are what make the game legendary.

### The Bad: Challenges and Frustrations

* **Anti-Cheat Issues:** Despite the introduction of "VAC Live," the game continues to struggle with cheaters in higher ranks. Many long-time players feel that the current anti-cheat system is insufficient to handle the evolving complexity of external software.
* **Performance Inconsistency:** While the Source 2 engine looks great, it demands more from hardware than its predecessor. Many players with mid-range setups have experienced inconsistent frame rates (stuttering) that can be fatal in a competitive shooter.
* **Content Deficit:** Since its release, many legacy maps, community game modes (like "Arms Race" or "Danger Zone" variations), and specific tactical elements from CS:GO have been slow to return or are missing entirely, leading to a sense of "less content" compared to the refined state CS:GO reached before its retirement.

---

### Final Verdict

Counter-Strike 2 is a foundation-level upgrade. It successfully brings the franchise into the modern era with better visuals and smarter utility mechanics. However, it still carries the weight of a transition period. While the core gameplay remains the "gold standard" of tactical shooters, the community is still waiting for Valve to refine the anti-cheat and bring back the depth of content that made the previous iteration feel so complete.

Counter-Strike 2 feels less like a competitive shooter and more like a social experiment designed to test how much suffering a player can endure before uninstalling.

The anti-cheat situation is so bad that every match feels like a coin flip between playing Counter-Strike and starring in a live demonstration of "How Walls Work." Trust Factor? Nobody knows what it does anymore. Good players get punished, questionable players get rewarded, and everyone gets thrown into the same digital dumpster fire.

Then there are the servers. Nothing says "premier competitive experience" quite like dying three business days after reaching cover. Every gunfight feels like you're arguing with the server about what actually happened.

And let's talk about communication from Valve. The community reports problems for months, and the response often feels like a mysterious silence broken only by another case release. Bugs survive longer than most esports careers.

As for Gabe Newell, at this point I picture him as a giant greedy fox sitting on a mountain of case keys, occasionally peeking down at the player base and saying, "Have you considered opening another crate instead of fixing the game?"

CS2 somehow took one of the greatest competitive games ever made and turned it into a trust-factor lottery running on servers powered by wishful thinking.

Recommended? Only if your hobbies include packet loss, existential despair, and trying to determine whether your opponent has incredible game sense or just a second monitor showing the entire map.

Counter-Strike is, without a doubt, the greatest game of all time for me. I've been playing Counter-Strike for over 20 years, and no other game has managed to keep me coming back for so long.

Over the years, I've met some amazing people through this game. Some of them became close friends, and a few I even met in real life. Very few games can create connections like that.

The gameplay is still fantastic. The movement feels responsive and satisfying, and the hit registration and feedback are usually instant and accurate. It's easy to get into, but incredibly difficult to master, which is one of the reasons why Counter-Strike remains relevant after all these years.

The maps are excellent, ranging from timeless classics to the occasional new and exciting community-made maps that keep things fresh. The graphics and the Source 2 engine are also a clear improvement and provide a modern look without sacrificing the core Counter-Strike experience.

Would I recommend Counter-Strike 2?

Honestly, I would — if it weren't for several major issues.

The cheating problem remains one of the biggest flaws of the game. Even worse, casual modes such as Deathmatch and Arms Race have become infested with bots to the point where they are practically unplayable at times. The overall selection of casual game modes is also surprisingly limited for a game of this size and age.

What makes this especially frustrating is the impression that Valve is either unwilling or unable to meaningfully address the cheating and bot problems. From a player's perspective, there seem to be very few effective measures being taken, while update after update focuses heavily on new skins and cosmetics.

What started as an incredible local multiplayer experience during my youth now feels like it's slowly crashing into the ground. Meanwhile, players are expected to get excited about the next case, sticker, or weapon finish.

Another thing that has changed for me is the whole case-opening experience. It simply doesn't feel rewarding anymore. What used to be an exciting little bonus has become something I barely care about nowadays. Opening cases no longer gives me the sense of anticipation or satisfaction it once did, making the constant focus on skins and cosmetics feel even more disconnected from the issues that actually affect the gameplay experience.

In the end, Counter-Strike 2 is still an amazing game at its core. The foundation is as strong as ever, and I will continue to play it. However, in its current state, I simply cannot recommend it to new players.

Dota 2 is a free-to-play game developed by people who apparently asked themselves, "What if chess was played by five screaming strangers who all think they're military geniuses?"

The game starts simply enough. You pick a hero. Then within five minutes, you're being blamed for events that happened before you were born.

Missed one last hit? Trash.

Died once? Reported.

Won your lane? Doesn't matter. Your carry is currently farming the jungle while the enemy destroys your Ancient and typing, "gg team no support."

The learning curve of Dota 2 isn't a curve. It's a vertical concrete wall coated in cooking oil. New players enter a match and immediately discover there are 100+ heroes, hundreds of abilities, dozens of items, countless mechanics, and approximately 4 million ways to embarrass themselves in front of strangers.

The community is one of the greatest social experiments ever conducted. Nowhere else can you find five people with completely different backgrounds united by a shared belief that every loss is somebody else's fault.

A typical Dota 2 match consists of:

One guy who thinks he's the next world champion.
One guy playing music through his microphone.
One guy whose internet is powered by a hamster.
One guy who hasn't spoken all game but suddenly writes a 500-word essay explaining why everyone else is terrible.
And you, wondering why you didn't just watch a movie instead.

The game is so addictive that players will spend 60 minutes suffering through the most miserable match imaginable, swear they'll never play again, close the game, stare at the desktop for 30 seconds, and immediately queue for another match.

The heroes themselves are absurd. Some are gods, dragons, demons, and ancient cosmic entities capable of destroying worlds. Yet all of them can be beaten to death by a shirtless guy with an axe who runs at people screaming.

The matchmaking system deserves its own award. Somehow it consistently creates games where both teams are convinced they received the worse players.

Dota 2 isn't a game.

It's a relationship.

A toxic, emotionally damaging relationship that occasionally gives you one incredible victory just to keep you from leaving.

And that's why millions of players keep coming back.

Because deep down, every Dota player believes the next game will be different.

It won't.

Its a game with a dangerous combination, its quite addicting but fundamentally broken at a root level, perhaps by design.

The game itself at its core is fun, the heroes are fun to play, and the game is updated semi-often (although the quality and quantity of said updates has significantly declined in the last few years).

Theirs no game quite like Dota 2, theirs over 100 heroes, all of them play completely differently, with their own skills and item builds, no two heroes feel the game. When playing with a stack theirs quite alot of thought that goes into your draft, your item build and your skill build. When it clicks its very addictive and quite honestly very fun. Nothing gives you a better dopamine hit than getting a rampage. Or winning that really close 50 minute game. 

But good lord the games horribly designed, to begin with, this game is unbelievably complicated, staring at the screen, youll see numbers and graphics everywhere, even basic skills and abilities can have half a page of text explaining what they do, items can too.  

This isnt a casual game that you play for a little while and move on, this is a game you play for life, or you dont play it at all. Even before you pick a hero to play, the fundamental basics of the game take months to learn, your looking at years of investment before your anywhere close to "good", thats just how complicated and in-depth this game is. 

If you want to play a new hero for example, youll need to read guides, watch videos and replays. You might be ok on a hero initially, but without going off and doing a bunch of research, you'll just end up throwing games and having people rage at you, this isnt a game, its a second job, in most cases it feels like your primary job. 

Then theirs the large patches that come out every 2-3 months, Dota 2 patches can be quite big. Dozens of pages and notes affecting huge amounts of heroes, items and even the map. Every time a release comes out you may have your favourite item or hero completely reworked entirely, meaning you effectively have to learn them again every 6-12 months, depending on the hero. Even worse, some patches completely change the basics of the game so drastically it feels like your playing a whole new game, this happens often.  

But perhaps the biggest design flaw of this game is the way it handles advantages in the early and mid game. When you get kills, you get money and experience, same with towers. Money lets you buy items to get stronger, experience helps you level up so you can get more stats and abilities. If one team gets an early lead, assuming a somewhat equal draft, then coming back is almost impossible since just being ahead gives you an advantage so you can get even more ahead, Dota 2 is an EXTREMELY snowball heavy game, once the snowball starts rolling, stopping it becomes almost impossible. 

The old saying "whoever gets ahead stays ahead" should be the motto of this game. In the rare case you do manage to pull off a comeback, its because the enemy team has made a series of major mistakes to let your team back in, rarely is it because you “outplayed” anyone.

This snowball methodology becomes so laughable that even if you do outplay the other team, you often wont get a kill just because the enemy team is so tanky, and your own items are so far behind that kills becomes significantly more difficult. The game actively prohibits better teams winning if they lose the mid/eary game because they are just too far behind to catchup. Cores with a gold/experience lead can legitimately wipe 3-4 enemy heroes on their own. 

Think of it this way, your playing tennis and you get a break of serve, your now ahead, as a result of you getting that break of serve, your own serve is now 25% faster, you move 25% quicker and your 25% less tired. This is the basic premise in Dota 2, you get a significant advantage just for being ahead, this happens in no other sport, you dont get to move 25% faster just because you sunk a three pointer in basketball. You dont get to throw a pitch 25% faster because you just struck someone out previously in a game of baseball. 

Moreover, stomps are VERY common in this game. 4/5 games are stomps where you know whose going to win after the first 10 or so minutes, where Dota 2 shines is that 1/5 game that goes down to the wire and you win. The addiction comes when you try to chase that same feeling and game for the next 3 days in vain. 

The other critical flaw in this game is just how minimal you can feel in terms of impact. You are 1 of 10 players, so even though you may be playing a great game, it doesnt matter if two other people on your team are just playing for laughs and giggles and end up dying alot in the early part of the game. Conversely, youll often win games where you play terribly, because someone else in your team is stomping everyone else. The only role that is absolutely critical is the position 1 role, you can win games with bad supports or an average mid, but you wont win with a terrible position 1. This often means that support players often feel like wins are out of their hands, it can be incredibly deflating when your playing fantastic as a support, but your position 1 feed 5 kills in the opening 2 minutes. 

The other aspect of this game that often gets overlooked is just how toxic games can be. This isnt COD or BF2 where games last 15 minutes, you can leave whenever you want and no one really talks because its just a goofy, fun game where no one really cares that much. Dota 2 games can last 50 minutes, thats a long time to be stuck with the same 4 people on your team, if things are going badly, people can get toxic very quickly, and you cant leave or quit before the game ends  since theres no surrender button. If your behind as per my above point, comebacks just dont happen that often, and as a result its not uncommon to be sitting in a game that was over 15 minutes ago, just watching you and your team mates die over and over again for 20 minutes. 

This game brings out the worst in people, you absolutely have to have very thick skin to play this game, its not for the timid or shy. 

In the end, I have over 9000 hours in this game, most of the time I have not enjoyed, but due to how addicting it can be, stopping becomes challenging. If you do take the plunge and dedicate serious amounts of time and effort into this game, quitting becomes even harder because youve already dedicated a huge amount of time already, time you dont want to feel like youve "wasted". 

I often think about what I could have done with those 9000 hours, what skills I could have developed or interests I could have pursued. Dont be like me, I hate this game and I wish I never played it.

Until 2022, it was an excellent game. 
After 2022, it has been in constant decline. 
Constant small and major “updates” keep making the game worse.

Matchmaking
The matchmaking randomness is insane — the chance of winning or losing feels like 50/50.
You can lose 10 matches in a row, then win 10 in a row.
Your personal skill has almost no impact on the outcome. 
There is a constant feeling that you have no control over the game, even if you receive the “Best Player of the Match” title more often than other players.

Hack-and-slash
The game has turned from a strategy game into a hack-and-slash.
From “play smart” to “play as a crowd.”
Victory no longer goes to the more skillful player, but to the team that can bring more allies to a fight at the right moment. You have become COMPLETELY dependent on your teammates.

The International 2025
This led to The International 2025 becoming the longest tournament in the game's history.
The best players of the world - Teams were so afraid to take fights without all five players present that five matches turned into around ten team fights stretched across five hours. Even the commentators did not seem happy, because there was almost nothing happening in the game to talk about.

Play every day
Every “update” drastically changes several random heroes.
So if you don’t play every day, but only once a week, you will constantly be unpleasantly surprised when your hero suddenly dies for no apparent reason.
The reason is simple: you were not prepared for the “new mechanic” introduced in the latest weekly update.
And yes, you will have to search YouTube for information about the “new updates” just to understand why your hero died.
The experience and mastery you accumulated with a character become meaningless because of the constant radical changes introduced in weekly “updates.”

Dear Valve Team,

I would like to give you a suggestion that concerns all Dota 2 players.

I believe the current reporting system should be reconsidered because it has made the game very frustrating. At the moment, anyone can report anyone, and in my experience this creates many unfair situations. I have been playing in what many players call the "hidden pool" for almost two years, and I have not been able to get out of it. Whether I win or lose, I continue to receive negative reports regardless of how I actually play.

I think there should simply be a mute option for communication issues. If someone does not like the way another player communicates, they can mute that person and continue playing. However, when a player becomes completely muted by the system, they can no longer communicate with teammates, which often makes teamwork much harder and can negatively affect the outcome of the game.

Please take this feedback into consideration. I have been playing Dota since the very beginning, dating back to the original Dota map in Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne. I care deeply about this game and want it to remain enjoyable for everyone.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
A longtime Dota player ❤️

Title: The best game you will ever hate.Rating: 10/10 (1,500+ hours on record)"Dota 2 isn’t just a video game; it’s a lifestyle, a second language, and a form of voluntary psychological torture.The premise is incredibly simple: two teams of five, three lanes, destroy the enemy's Ancient. With over 120 completely unique heroes and hundreds of items, no two matches are ever the same. You don't 'master' Dota; you just get slightly less bad at it over the span of five years.  It features some of the most rewarding highs in all of gaming. Landing a perfect five-man teamfight or turning around a 60-minute base siege gives you an absolute rush that no other multiplayer game can replicate. On the flip side, it also features some of the lowest lows—like when your teammate picks a carry hero as a support and leaves you to suffer alone in lane.The community is notoriously intense, but when you find a team that clicks, it’s magic. Best of all, it is truly free-to-play. Every single hero is unlocked from day one, and money only buys you cosmetic hats.If you value your free time, your sanity, and your sleep schedule, stay far away. Grand Theft Auto V is one of those games that became massive for a reason.

The story is wild, the characters are ridiculous, the world is huge, and Los Santos is still one of the best playgrounds for pure open-world chaos. You can follow the missions like a normal person, or you can immediately get distracted stealing a car, driving off a mountain, starting a police chase, buying clothes, playing golf, or just roaming around causing problems because the map gave you too much freedom and not enough supervision.

That is the magic of GTA V.

The game gives you crime, comedy, action, satire, driving, shooting, chaos, and a city that feels alive enough to keep pulling you away from whatever you originally planned to do. One minute you are doing a serious heist setup, the next minute you are in a stolen sports car with three stars, no plan, and the confidence of someone who definitely should not be driving.

The three-character story setup works really well too. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor all bring something different, and switching between them makes the game feel bigger and more chaotic in the best way. Trevor especially is a walking public safety warning with dialogue.

GTA Online is its own beast, and honestly, that can either be amazing or deeply cursed depending on who you run into. But the base game alone is still packed with so much to do.

Grand Theft Auto V is messy, funny, violent, iconic, and ridiculously easy to lose hours in.

Sometimes you want a deep emotional journey. Sometimes you want to steal a car, launch it off a ramp, and pretend that was the plan.

GTA 5 is one of those games that feels impossible to review normally because it’s not just a game anymore, it’s basically a whole era of gaming. This game came out in 2013 and somehow still feels more alive than half the games that come out today with “next-gen” slapped on the box.

The story is still fire. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor all represent different types of chaos. Michael is the washed-up rich guy who “made it” but is still miserable. Franklin is trying to level up and escape the same street cycle. Trevor is just pure unfiltered demon energy. That three-character system still works because each of them gives you a different lens on Los Santos, and Los Santos itself is probably the real main character.

The map is insane. You can be in the hood, downtown, the hills, the desert, the mountains, the beach, or some random gas station in the middle of nowhere and it all feels like it has a purpose. Rockstar cooked with the atmosphere. Driving around at night listening to the radio still hits different. It has that weird feeling where even if you’re doing nothing, you’re still entertained.

The gameplay is simple but addictive. Shooting, driving, flying, robbing stores, causing chaos, running from cops, doing missions, buying cars, customizing weapons — it’s all easy to get lost in. And honestly, that’s the magic of GTA. You can play it like a serious crime movie or you can play it like a complete idiot and both are valid.

GTA Online is a different beast. It’s fun, but it also became this wild grind machine where everything costs millions and half the lobby is flying around on weaponized alien bikes like it’s no longer GTA, it’s capitalism with missiles. Still, with friends, it’s hilarious. Alone, it can feel like a second job.

My only real criticism is that Rockstar milked this game like crazy. GTA 5 is legendary, but bro, we were stuck with it for over a decade. At some point it became less “wow this game is timeless” and more “please release GTA 6 before society collapses.”

Overall, GTA 5 is still one of the greatest open-world games ever made. It has story, freedom, chaos, vibes, replay value, and that rare feeling where the world actually feels alive. It’s not perfect, and GTA Online got ridiculous, but the base game is certified legendary.

I thought I was starting a game about killing monsters.

Instead, I found a story about family, love, friendship, loss, and the people we would cross the world for.

Geralt's journey to find Ciri is one of the most memorable stories I've experienced in gaming. But what truly made this adventure special were the people around him. Yennefer and Triss aren't just romance options on a menu; they're characters who feel real. They have flaws, dreams, fears, and histories that make every interaction meaningful.

There were moments that made me smile, moments that broke my heart, and moments that made me sit quietly and think about the choices I had made. Few games manage to make you care this much.

The world is beautiful, but its greatest strength is its soul. From the muddy roads of Velen to the icy winds of Skellige, every place feels alive. Every quest feels like someone's story rather than another task to complete.

When the credits rolled, I wasn't thinking about the monsters I had slain or the loot I had collected.

I was thinking about Ciri.

I was thinking about Yennefer.

I was thinking about Triss.

I was thinking about the friends I met and the goodbyes I never wanted to say.

The Witcher 3 didn't feel like a game I finished. It felt like a world I had to leave behind.

❤️ "In a world full of monsters, the only thing worth fighting for is the people we love."
For those returning to the game because of the new DLC, remember, silver is for monsters and steel is for fools.

After 10 years, this game still looks better than some brand-new releases today. On the highest settings, it sometimes feels like a fantasy vacation with ray tracing instead of sunscreen. 🌲⚔️
You ride peacefully through the world, admire the scenery… and suddenly get jumped by some monster hiding in the bushes. 10/10 atmosphere.
The story? Absolutely brilliant. It feels like playing an interactive fantasy book — except every now and then you beat people up with two swords. Every quest somehow has its own little story, and even the side quests are often more exciting than the entire main stories of other games.
And then there are the DLCs…
With Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine, it honestly feels like you’re getting an entire extra game. Hours upon hours of additional fun, new areas, new characters, and even more reasons why you wanted to do “just one more quest”… and suddenly it’s 3 AM.
Small downside:
Sometimes the gameplay turns into “Ride from ? to ? and clear 17 bandit camps along the way.” The grinding can occasionally get a bit annoying. But at least even riding around looks gorgeous.

I had played this game before and finished it, but it never truly clicked with me. So I decided to start a new save file, this time on a higher difficulty, with a commitment to fully immerse myself in every mechanic the game had to offer.

And boy, what a game.

The atmosphere is nothing short of fantastic. I could listen to the soundtrack for hours on end, and the visuals still look stunning for an 11-year-old game. The characters are genuine and memorable, starting with the protagonist himself, Geralt. Every quest feels meaningful and well-crafted, and I even developed a genuine love for Gwent, something that was completely absent in my first playthrough. By the end, I truly felt like a witcher.

10/10 — An Absolute Masterpiece.

Probably one of my favorite games of all time. For how old the game is at this point it still looks great at the time of this review. The story is amazing, and even the side quests have more plot than main story missions in other AAA titles. The games makes you think critically, and not just assume things at face value, it is very easy to assume something is bad just because it is a monster, but you can talk to a lot of them and realize they're sentient in a lot of cases and not harmful to humans. You could easily go through the game just killing everything, but I really appreciate the nuance the game has when it comes to determining your enemy if you want to look into things more. Humans can often be more monstrous than some of the actual monsters throughout the game.

A game that puts its predecessors to shame. There is a massive leap forward in gameplay, graphics, and world-building compared to the first two games in the series. The introduction is far better as well; the prologue is short, sweet, and does a wonderful job at introducing all of the game mechanics and gets you up to speed on the story, something the previous game sorely lacked.

The world is massive and alive. Cities are densely populated, while the numerous villages, keeps, and smaller communities all have their own people and stories. With all these characters comes a wealth of side-quests, most of which are interesting and well written. If you are someone who likes to complete everything, Act 1 can be quite daunting, as you are dropped into the world with seemingly endless content, which adds significantly to the game’s length.

As with the previous games, the story is very well written and extremely well paced. “Tension” is the word I would use to describe it best, as it does a fantastic job keeping you hooked and invested. You can complete it in many different ways and in many different orders, and the developers have foreseen a lot of unpredictable and interesting routes you can take.

The new alchemy system is much better than in previous instalments. Once you craft a potion or oil, you only need to meditate to refill it. Crafting has also improved, but still felt a little tedious, especially towards the end of the game. Skills and mutagens allow you to customize your playstyle and it felt like there were very few filler unlocks.

Gone are the days of dice poker and the annoying RNG behind it, as it has been replaced with something far superior: Gwent. This card game can be like crack to the right person, and it was truly a joy collecting every card and building every deck. Alas, as you start to get further into the game, you can effectively solve Gwent, which detracts from the enjoyment. It still remains one of the greatest mini-games I’ve ever encountered in an RPG.

The DLC deserve their own reviews, but I will briefly mention them here:
[list]
[*] Hearts of Stone is a small, but thrilling story with a lot of surprises and had me swinging like a pendulum when picking sides. The return of an old friend was great and certainly adds a lot if 	you are a longtime fan of the games.

[*] Blood & Wine is a truly masterful DLC in a beautiful setting. In my opinion, the story surpasses the base game, and the side content is great as well. The player housing is a great touch and finally gives Geralt a place to call home.
[/list]
Overall, I am not sure why I waited so long to play this game. Even over ten years later, it holds up remarkably well and stands out as one of the greatest RPGs of all time.

When I first started playing The Witcher 3, I found the game quite dark and difficult to understand. The world, the politics, the characters, and the lore can feel overwhelming at first. However, if you are willing to be patient and persevere, everything slowly starts to make sense. Once you truly understand the world and the environment you are playing in, the experience becomes incredibly rewarding.

As for the gameplay, I really enjoyed the combat system. It reminds me somewhat of games like Dark Souls or Elden Ring, although it is obviously much more accessible and less punishing. The combat remains engaging throughout the entire adventure and allows players to approach encounters in different ways.

One of the things that impressed me the most is the amount of customization available. The Witcher 3 is one of the rare modern games that still offers such a wide variety of weapons, armor sets, character builds, skills, and statistics. Everything feels deep and meaningful. The progression system is incredibly complete and gives players a lot of freedom in how they want to develop Geralt.

I also loved the collection aspect of the game. Being able to improve your horse, collect trophies from defeated monsters, and search for rare equipment constantly gives you new objectives to pursue. There is always something to discover, upgrade, or collect.

Another reason why The Witcher 3 is so exceptional is the impact of player choice. Very few games manage to make dialogue choices feel as important as they do here. Your decisions can significantly affect the story, the relationships between characters, and even the ending itself. This is one of the main reasons why I became so attached to the game. Every choice feels meaningful, and you genuinely feel responsible for the consequences.

The world map is also massive and incredibly detailed. You can simply wander around without following the main story and constantly stumble upon side quests, hidden locations, and unexpected adventures. What makes these side quests special is that they rarely feel like simple filler content. Most of them have interesting stories, memorable characters, and sometimes even reward you with rare and powerful loot.

The DLC expansions deserve special recognition as well. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine are not only outstanding expansions, but they could honestly be considered complete games on their own. They introduce new stories, new locations, memorable characters, and dozens of hours of additional content. Together, they can easily provide over fifty hours of gameplay, making them some of the best DLCs ever created.

Regarding the graphics, they are beginning to show their age slightly, but not by much. In my opinion, modern AAA games are not dramatically more impressive visually. The Witcher 3 still looks fantastic today, especially thanks to the next-generation update and the option to enable ray tracing. The environments remain beautiful, atmospheric, and immersive.

To conclude this review, I first discovered The Witcher 3 alongside my uncle when I was younger. Many years later, I decided to experience the game again on Steam. It is one of the very few games that came close to making me cry. The story deeply moved me and will always hold a special place in my heart.

I wholeheartedly recommend The Witcher 3 to anyone looking for a long, rich, and unforgettable adventure. It is a game where your choices truly matter, where every journey feels unique, and where you can become the Geralt you want to be.

Thank you, CD Projekt Red.

Thank you for this incredible story.

And thank you for giving me so many unforgettable memories.

After spending more than 100 hours in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, I can confidently say this is one of the greatest games ever made.

From the moment you step into the world as Geralt of Rivia, you're immersed in a living, breathing world filled with unforgettable characters, meaningful choices, and stories that are often better than entire games. What amazed me most is how even the smallest side quests felt handcrafted and emotionally engaging. There were countless moments where a simple contract or random encounter turned into a memorable adventure.

The world is absolutely stunning. Whether you're wandering through the war-torn fields of Velen, exploring the bustling streets of Novigrad, or sailing across the beautiful islands of Skellige, every location feels unique and packed with detail. The writing is phenomenal. Geralt, Yennefer, Triss, Ciri, and the Bloody Baron are some of the most well-written characters I've encountered in gaming. The choices you make actually matter, and many of them don't have a clear "right" answer, making the experience feel incredibly personal.

The soundtrack deserves special praise as well. The music perfectly captures the atmosphere of every region and has become one of my favorite game soundtracks of all time.

And then there are the expansions. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine are not just DLCs—they're masterpieces in their own right and offer more quality content than many full-priced games.

Even years after release, The Witcher 3 remains the benchmark for open-world RPGs. Few games have managed to match its storytelling, world-building, and attention to detail.

Few games manage to achieve the level of quality, immersion, and craftsmanship found in The Witcher 3. From the very beginning, the game demonstrates an extraordinary level of attention to detail. The world feels alive, authentic, and carefully constructed, with every region offering its own atmosphere, culture, and stories. Whether exploring bustling cities, war-torn villages, dense forests, or remote islands, players are constantly rewarded with meaningful discoveries and memorable encounters.
      The narrative is undoubtedly one of the game's greatest strengths. The main story is thoughtfully written, emotionally engaging, and filled with compelling characters whose motivations and development feel believable throughout the adventure. What truly sets the game apart, however, is the quality of its side content. Unlike many open-world titles where optional missions feel repetitive or insignificant, side quests here are often as captivating as the main storyline itself. Each quest is carefully crafted, frequently presenting players with difficult choices and consequences that add depth to the overall experience.
      The gameplay is equally impressive. Combat encounters strike an excellent balance between accessibility and challenge, while the variety of enemies, abilities, and character builds ensures that the experience remains fresh throughout the journey. Some quests and battles are relatively straightforward, allowing players to enjoy the narrative and exploration, while others provide a more demanding challenge that rewards preparation and skill. This variation contributes significantly to the game's exceptional pacing and long-term engagement.
     One of the most remarkable aspects of this game is its ability to captivate the player for extended periods of time. It is the kind of game that constantly encourages "just one more quest," making it incredibly easy to lose track of time while exploring its vast world. Every completed objective naturally leads to another intriguing mystery, contract, or storyline, creating an experience that is both immersive and highly addictive in the best possible sense.
     The technical and artistic execution further elevates the experience. The visual design remains impressive even by modern standards, while the soundtrack perfectly complements the atmosphere of each location and story moment. Together, these elements create a world that feels both believable and unforgettable.
     In conclusion, The Witcher 3 is a remarkable achievement in game design and storytelling. Its exceptional narrative, engaging quests, rewarding gameplay, and extraordinary attention to detail combine to create an experience that few games can match. Based on my experience so far, it has been nothing short of fantastic. I can confidently recommend it to anyone looking for a truly high-quality role-playing game and one of the most memorable adventures the gaming industry has ever produced.

Some games entertain you. Some games impress you. Very few games make you forget you're sitting in front of a screen.

The Witcher 3 is one of those rare games.

What surprised me most isn't the size of the world or the graphics—it's how believable everything feels. Villages have their own stories, random encounters feel meaningful, and even the smallest side activities often have more care put into them than entire questlines in other games.

The game doesn't treat the player like a hero at the center of the universe. Instead, it drops you into a world that already exists and lets you find your place in it. The result is a setting that feels alive rather than built around a checklist of objectives.

Combat, exploration, music, atmosphere, characters, dialogue—everything works together to create an adventure that is incredibly easy to get lost in. Hours disappear without you noticing because every road leads to something interesting, whether it's a mystery, a difficult choice, or simply a beautiful landscape worth stopping to admire.

It's rare for a game to feel this handcrafted. Even years after release, it's easy to understand why so many people still consider it one of the greatest RPGs ever made.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is one of the best open-world RPG games ever made. The story follows Geralt of Rivia, a monster hunter searching for his adopted daughter in a dark and dangerous world.

Overall, The Witcher 3 is a masterpiece and a must-play game for anyone who enjoys RPGs and story-driven games.

Side quests often feel better than main stories in other RPGs.
Choices have real consequences, sometimes hours later.

Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine are among the best expansions ever released.

Combat is serviceable but not the game's strongest feature.

The first few hours may feel overwhelming due to the number of systems and quests.

The Witcher 3 is the complete package: an incredible story, memorable characters, meaningful choices, and hundreds of hours of content. Even years after release, it remains the benchmark for story-driven open-world RPGs.

Stardew Valley is somehow considered one of the most relaxing games ever made, but after playing long enough you realize it’s actually just an anxiety simulator disguised as a cute farming game.

People say:
“Just chill and enjoy the farm life.”

Meanwhile the game has you speedrunning your entire existence every single day because apparently 14 in-game minutes pass every time your character blinks.

Wake up.
Water crops.
Feed animals.
Check machines.
Collect eggs.
Talk to villagers.
Mine rocks.
Fish.
Forage.
Donate museum items.
Upgrade tools.
Rush home before 2 AM or collapse like a Victorian child dying from exhaustion.

Very relaxing.

The game constantly pretends to be cozy while secretly turning players into optimization addicts. Nobody starts Stardew Valley saying:
“I need maximum sprinkler efficiency and ancient fruit wine profit margins.”

But 30 hours later people are calculating crop rotations like they’re managing an agricultural hedge fund.

And the stamina system in early game is torture.
You chop down three trees and your farmer already looks ready for hospice care. Want to clear your farm?
Too bad.
Your character gets exhausted faster than someone climbing stairs after eating an entire pizza.

The villagers are also weirdly overrated.
Everyone talks about how “deep” and “heartwarming” they are, but half the town acts rude until you bribe them with vegetables twice a week.

“Oh wow thanks for giving me this random flower.
Now I no longer hate your existence.”

Groundbreaking social design.

And somehow every villager has the same schedule complexity as a CIA operative. Miss someone by 10 minutes?
Congratulations, now they’ve vanished into another dimension until tomorrow.

Fishing is another crime against humanity.
People either love it or want to throw their monitor through a wall. Why is catching a tiny fish harder than landing a spacecraft? Early-game fishing feels like wrestling a possessed bottle cap using pure disappointment.

Then there’s the mines.
Which are somehow:

* repetitive
* stressful
* grindy
* and weirdly mandatory

Because eventually the game stops being:
“cute farming adventure”
and becomes:
“industrial resource extraction simulator.”

Your beautiful little farm slowly transforms into a capitalist machine full of kegs, furnaces, preserve jars, crystalariums, and enough automation to concern labor unions.

And don’t even get me started on Pierre.
The entire community collectively agrees that Pierre sucks, and honestly that’s probably the most emotionally united the playerbase has ever been.

The calendar system is pure psychological warfare too.
Forget one birthday and suddenly an NPC dislikes you for the next century because you didn’t hand them mayonnaise on exactly the correct Tuesday.

The game also pressures you constantly with seasonal timing:

* missed crop season
* missed event
* missed fish
* missed recipe
* missed bundle item

Oops.
Guess you wait an entire in-game year now.

Fantastic.

And despite the cute graphics, the gameplay loop becomes disturbingly repetitive:

* wake up
* harvest crops
* refill machines
* organize inventory
* sleep
* repeat until real life seasons change too

The soundtrack is amazing though.
Which honestly feels intentional because the music is probably the only reason players don’t realize they’ve spent 6 real-life hours optimizing blueberry production.

The craziest thing about Stardew Valley is that it successfully convinces millions of people that doing farm chores after work is somehow a form of relaxation.

You’re not escaping responsibilities.
You’re just replacing your real responsibilities with pixel responsibilities.

[h1]"Just one more day..."[/h1]
[hr][/hr]

I bought this game thinking, "Oh, a cute little pixel-art farming simulator. I'll play it for twenty minutes to unwind after a stressful day."

Next thing I knew, it was 4:00 AM. I had three spreadsheets open on my phone, a fully optimized automatic sprinkler system mapped out, and I was genuinely angry at a fictional pixelated blacksmith named Clint for closing his shop at 4:00 PM when I desperately needed to break open some geodes.

This isn't just a game; it’s a beautifully crafted escape from reality.

[h4]The Good Stuff:[/h4]
-The Gameplay Loop: It is absolute perfection. Wake up, water crops, check the weather, pet your chickens, forage, fish, or head into the mines to fight monsters. Every single day feels productive, and just when you think you're ready to log off, you realize tomorrow is a festival or your crops are about to harvest. You will get trapped in the "one more day" cycle.
-The Value: For the price of a fast-food meal, you get hundreds of hours of base-game content, massive free content updates that could easily have been paid DLCs, multiplayer co-op, and a massive modding community if you ever somehow run out of things to do.

[h4]The Cons:[/h4]
-Time completely ceases to exist in the real world while playing.
-Your real-life relationships might suffer because you're too busy trying to figure out what purple items to put in the Mayor's soup.
-Meeting your crush at the Flower Dance in Year 1 just to have them say "Ew, no." hits harder than any Dark Souls boss.

[h4]Final Verdict:[/h4]
If you are stressed, burnt out, or just need to feel something wholesome again, buy this game. It will heal your soul, steal your time, and teach you how to love raising a virtual duck named Howard.

Before I played Stardew Valley, I never thought pixel art could captivate me. I always gravitated toward modern, realistic graphics, the kind that try to impress you with detail and fidelity. But Stardew Valley changed that completely. Its simplicity isn’t a limitation, it’s a kind of magic. The pixel art feels warm, nostalgic, and alive in a way I didn’t expect, and it opened my eyes to an entire style of games I used to overlook.

Even though I haven’t played much on PC or mobile yet, my Switch farm has over 500 hours poured into it. It’s perfected, polished, and complete… and yet, I still feel the pull to go back. There’s something comforting about stepping onto that farm again, hearing the soft music, and slipping back into the rhythm of planting, harvesting, mining, and connecting with the townsfolk.

What makes Stardew Valley special is how personal it becomes. It doesn’t rush you. It doesn’t demand anything. It simply invites you to build a life at your own pace and somehow, that quiet freedom becomes deeply meaningful. Whether it’s the changing seasons, the relationships you build, or the satisfaction of watching your farm evolve, the game creates a sense of home that’s rare to find.

Even after “finishing” it, I still want to revisit it often. That’s the mark of a truly great game: one that stays with you long after the goals are completed.

I bought Stardew Valley thinking it would be a nice little farming game to play now and then.

Instead, it somehow became a game where I spend hours saying "just one more day" before realising it's way later than I planned.

What I love most is that you can do whatever you feel like. Some days I'm farming, some days I'm fishing, some days I'm down in the mines getting beaten up by serpents, and some days I'm completely ignoring my farm while I run around trying to complete random quests.

The amount of content in this game is honestly ridiculous for the price. I've paid more for a single DLC in other games than I paid for Stardew Valley, yet this game has given me far more enjoyment.

I also love that it doesn't feel like it's constantly trying to sell me something. You buy the game and that's it. No endless DLC, no battle passes, no microtransactions. Just a genuinely brilliant game made by someone who clearly cares about the people playing it.

The characters are great, the music is relaxing, and somehow even doing virtual chores is fun.

My only warning is that this game will completely destroy your sense of time. You'll tell yourself you're only playing for 20 minutes and then suddenly it's dark outside and you've spent the evening trying to reach the bottom of the mines or reorganising your farm for the tenth time.

An absolute gem of a game and one I'll keep coming back to for years.

I've played Stardew Valley for over 1,000 hours, reached perfection, and started more farms than I can count. Somehow, after all these years, I still find myself coming back.

There are games that you enjoy for a while, and then there are games that quietly become part of your life. Stardew Valley is the latter for me.

The music has a way of calming me down no matter what kind of day I've had. The world feels like a place I can always return to, whether I want to build something new, chase a goal, or simply spend a peaceful evening tending crops and talking to villagers.

What makes this game even more special is the person behind it. Seeing one developer continue to pour so much love into a game through free updates, years after release, is incredibly rare. Every update feels like a gift from someone who genuinely cares about the community that formed around their creation.

But more than anything, Stardew Valley holds some of my favourite gaming memories. I've spent countless hours playing alongside my best friend, and many of those moments are memories I'll carry with me forever. When I think about Stardew Valley, I don't just think about farming, fishing, or reaching perfection. I think about laughter, late-night sessions, and a friendship that became intertwined with this little pixelated world.

It's difficult to put into words how much this game means to me. All I know is that after more than 1,000 hours, I'm still here.

And I suspect I always will be.

**Title: A Slice of Paradise in Stardew Valley**

Stardew Valley has completely transformed my gaming experience, and I feel compelled to share just how special this game truly is. From the moment I stepped onto my grandfather's farm, I was captivated by its charm and depth.

The first thing that strikes you about Stardew Valley is its beautiful pixel art. The landscapes are breathtaking, from the rolling hills and lush forests to the quaint town bustling with life. Each season brings its own vibrant palette, and watching the world change around me with the passing months adds a touch of magic to everyday activities. The attention to detail is incredible, with each character and location meticulously crafted to create an immersive environment.

The gameplay is a perfect blend of simplicity and complexity. At first glance, it may seem like a farming simulator, but Stardew Valley offers so much more. There’s a unique mix of farming, mining, crafting, and social interactions that keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging. Planting crops, raising animals, and expanding my farm are incredibly satisfying, especially when I see the fruits of my labor come to life. Managing my farm allows for creativity; I can design it however I want, making each player's experience unique.

What truly shines in Stardew Valley is the sense of community. The townsfolk are well-developed characters with their own stories, quirks, and routines. Building relationships with them, participating in festivals, and learning their secrets adds depth to the game. There’s something heartwarming about helping them out or just stopping by for a chat. The diverse cast ensures that there’s someone for everyone to connect with, and I genuinely found friendships with characters like Abigail, Harvey, and the wise old wizard.

The music and sound design also deserve a mention. The serene and soothing soundtrack perfectly complements the gameplay, creating an atmosphere that is both relaxing and enchanting. Whether I'm working late into the night on my farm or exploring the forgotten mines, the melodies enhance the experience and make even the simplest tasks feel rewarding.

The game’s progression system is rewarding without ever feeling punishing. There’s no rush, and players can progress at their own pace. Whether you want to focus on farming, mining, fishing, or engaging in the local economy, the choice is yours. The game encourages exploration and experimentation, which kept me engaged and excited to discover new aspects of the game.

Additionally, Stardew Valley excels in its multiplayer capabilities. Playing with friends adds a new dimension to the experience. We could work together on the farm, tackle some of the more challenging aspects of the game, or simply enjoy the company of each other as we go about our rural lives. It’s a delightful way to bond over shared goals and objectives.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterpiece that brings together engaging gameplay, charming aesthetics, and a warm sense of community. It’s the perfect escape from reality, allowing me to step into a world where I can unwind, explore, and create. There’s a peacefulness in tending to crops and making new friends that I never want to end, and I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone looking for a rewarding and heartwarming experience. Simply put, Stardew Valley is more than just a game; it’s a home away from home. 🌻🍓✨

Awesome game, a bit misunderstood and overhated at launch.

Graphics are incredible overall, especially after all the updates. Night City is one of the most detailed and immersive open worlds ever made, full of life, neon lights, crowded streets and beautiful environments. Character models and facial animations are excellent, and the combat animations feel fluid and satisfying. Some NPC behaviors can still feel a bit awkward at times, but the overall presentation is top tier.

Sound design is amazing. Weapons sound powerful, cars feel aggressive, the city ambience is immersive, and the voice acting is top tier across the board. The music is absolutely phenomenal, perfectly matching every moment, whether you're cruising through the city at night, fighting through chaos, or experiencing emotional story moments.

Gameplay is great and highly engaging. Let's start with the combat, because many people still think Cyberpunk is just "GTA with RPG elements", but it offers so much more than that. There are many different playstyles to choose from: stealth hacking, aggressive gunplay, melee combat, katanas, throwing knives, cyberware-focused builds, snipers, shotguns, netrunning, and more. Every build feels different and has strengths and weaknesses depending on your approach and preparation. Combat is fast, fluid and rewarding, especially once your build starts coming together. The movement also feels great, especially with double jumps, dashes and cyberware upgrades that make you feel increasingly powerful.
The progression system is great, allowing you to specialize heavily into your preferred playstyle. Skill trees offer meaningful upgrades that genuinely change how you approach combat and exploration. Cyberware customization is one of the best parts of the game, letting you turn your character into an unstoppable machine, stealth hacker, samurai or whatever style you prefer.
Looting and equipment are also very satisfying. Finding iconic weapons, upgrading cyberware and experimenting with builds keeps the gameplay fresh for dozens of hours.
Exploration is another huge strength. Night City feels alive and dense, with hidden events, side gigs, random encounters and environmental storytelling everywhere. Even just driving around the city at night can be immersive on its own.
The side content is surprisingly strong too. Many side quests are written with the same quality as the main story, often presenting difficult choices, morally gray situations and memorable characters. Some side quests end up being more emotionally impactful than entire main campaigns in other games.
Another great mechanic is how your choices and relationships affect quest outcomes, dialogue and endings. Some opportunities, conversations and endings are only available depending on how you played and who you connected with throughout the game.
These are only some of the great mechanics the game offers, the rest are for you to discover.

The enemies are varied and fun to fight. Different gangs use different weapons, tactics and cyberware, forcing you to adapt your approach. Boss fights and cyberpsychos can also be very memorable, especially when your build is tested properly.

The story is excellent, emotional and extremely well written. The characters are memorable, believable and full of personality. V and Johnny Silverhand have fantastic chemistry throughout the game, and many side characters leave a strong impression too. The role playing aspects are very well done, with meaningful dialogue choices, different character backgrounds and multiple endings depending on your decisions. The game constantly presents morally complex situations where there is rarely a completely right or wrong answer. Also some of the endings are brutal, so be prepared to a rollercoaster of emotions.

In short, awesome game, a bit misunderstood because of its disastrous launch. After years of updates and improvements, the game became what people originally hoped it would be. Many people still judge it based on old impressions without giving it another chance. If you enjoy immersive RPGs, great storytelling, strong world building and flexible character progression, this game is absolutely worth experiencing.

I believe i originally preordered this game way back in 2018, before it was delayed multiple times. By the time it came out, i wasn't even too broken up over the rough state the game was in. After years of waiting, the money i had spent on it hardly felt like it had ever existed. I played the game for 10 hours and then dropped it.

Fast Forward to 2026 and i get the urge to come give it another shot. I remembered enjoying the bit of the story I did get to experience, and i knew that the gameplay and bugginess of the game had been improved to various extents.

Having now binged nearly all of the content in the base game over the course of two weeks, i can confidently say that i am satisfied with my purchase of this game eight years ago. 
While occasionally rough around the edges, i did thoroughly enjoy the combat and character progression of the game. Running mostly a blade build let me enjoy an up close, frenetic combat style that i imagine to be wholly different but equally as enjoyable as to what might be experienced from focusing more on quickhacks or on smart weapons.
I found myself doing nearly all of the side jobs the game had to offer (save for the gigs, but i occasionally still did those if i stumbled into them), and was well satisfied with more of them than i would have expected. This is really all thanks to the character writing in this game. 

By far, the standout feature of Cyberpunk is its writing. Dialogue between characters feels natural and animations in important moments are incredibly well done. I found myself really invested in the relationships between many of the main cast, and especially the relationships that V has with Johnny, Panam and Judy. 
I won't speak on the endings too much, but i think they are all very well written. Something tells me that people were not happy with some of them when the game came out, but maybe i'm just being harsh on the average gamer in 2020.

I will say, the performance in the open world can sometimes be lacking, although i will admit that i run the game on ultra settings with a 2k monitor and average above 60 fps. I will especially mention that I never had any performance hiccups during important story scenes, I never once found myself taken out of a moment because of lag. The game also has occasional small bugs, like a cop walking around inside the sidewalk or a civilian loudly and repeatedly running their car into a wall 20 feet away from a conversation you're having. Nothing serious.

Honestly, my biggest complaint with the game is the content surrounding the romantic relationships in the game, or the lack of it. [spoiler] I can only speak on the relationship with Judy, but i imagine the others are quite the same. There's a whole big mission (and honestly a decent amount of setup in the background throughout the game) of this potential relationship blossoming, and once it finally does, the only thing that comes of it is occasional text conversations that eventually dry up, and a repeatable date mission in which you have access to a few small events and a set of dialogue that never changes and is largely the same as what you would get when you called Judy before you were even in a relationship. [/spoiler]
I think it speaks greatly to this game's strengths that this is my biggest issue with it.

I know this game has largely positive reviews today, but i imagine there are still a lot of people who view the game in the light it was (often justly) received in at launch (although there were certainly unrealistic expectations surrounding the game at the time as well). I hope any of those people who may have dropped the game like i did come give it another shot some time, it's really worth it.

Few games in history have undergone a redemption arc quite like Cyberpunk 2077. While its initial launch was famously rocky, CD Projekt RED’s unwavering commitment to their vision—culminating in the massive 2.0 update and the brilliant Phantom Liberty expansion—has officially transformed this game into a certified masterpiece.

Night City is the undisputed star of the show. It is a towering, neon-soaked vertical labyrinth that feels genuinely alive, dangerous, and intoxicating. Walking through the crowded streets of Watson or driving through the desolate Badlands offers an unparalleled level of environmental immersion. The world-building is incredibly dense, capturing the corporate-dominated, gritty essence of classic cyberpunk lore.

It is impossible to talk about the renaissance of this game without mentioning Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, the phenomenal Studio Trigger anime series. Edgerunners didn't just capture the hearts of fans; it perfectly mirrored the game's high-stakes, tragic, and adrenaline-fueled atmosphere.

The anime injected a massive wave of fresh energy into the game, making the exploration of Night City feel even more personal. Visiting locations featured in the show, listening to "I Really Want to Stay at Your House" on the in-game radio, or equipping David Martinez’s iconic jacket adds a profound layer of emotional depth for anyone who loved the series.

With the overhauled cyberware systems, revamped skill trees, and chaotic vehicle combat introduced in recent updates, the gameplay finally matches the narrative's ambition. Combat is fast, brutal, and highly customizable. Whether you want to be a stealthy Netrunner hacking enemies from afar or a sandevistan-powered solo slicing through corporate guards with a katana, the playstyles are incredibly rewarding.

At its core, the story of V and Johnny Silverhand is a deeply moving tale about legacy, identity, and survival against all odds.

Cyberpunk 2077 is no longer just a game about promises; it is a triumphant delivery of an unforgettable sci-fi RPG. If you were waiting for the right time to lose yourself in Night City—especially if you are a fan of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners—there has never been a better time to chrome up and dive in.

I have mixed feelings about this game but I decided to give it a positive review because I don't think it's bad but it's not great either. I had fun playing it but I expected much more. Here are some of my thoughts:

- The graphics are beautiful and I love the vibe of this game. The open world looks impressive, but when you try to explore it, you quickly discover that most buildings are inaccessible and few places are interactive.

- Unfortunately, I couldn't fully immerse myself in the main story. Dialogue options are very limited and only give you an illusion of actually influencing the story. I'm used to RPGs giving me a lot of options on how I want the story to progress so I was a bit disappointed. Cyberpunk reminds me more of games like Far Cry than typical RPGs and I guess I expected a different experience. I feel like it's more of a shooter than an RPG.

- Cutscenes and some quests can be very tiring and feel slow because in most of them you just listen to a character talk and follow them around or sit in a car with them.

- The game tries to create a sense of urgency but in reality there's no time limit and you can complete as many side quests as you want without affecting anything. Even missions that start with a character calling you and saying they'd like to meet you at a certain time today have no time limit and you can delay them for as long as you want.

- The romance is okay but a lot of things get repetitive and feel a bit mechanical. I romanced Judy and every time she visited my apartment, she said the exact same thing, no new dialogue appeared and nothing interesting happened. She was just there and that's it.

- I'm not a huge fan of Johnny Silverhand. I like the idea of his character but I feel like his potential wasn't fully realized and his relationship with V could have been more interesting. It was a bit strange to me how he suddenly went from being hostile towards V to being nice. Also, Keanu Reeves' performance in this role felt flat and emotionless at times.

- I dread to think how bad this game was when it first came out because even after all these years it's still very buggy. Disappearing NPCs, items getting stuck in NPCs' hands, messy AI that causes enemies to randomly pause during fights and allow you to kill them easily, enemies seeing you through walls, NPCs bugging so you're unable to talk to them when you want to start/finish a quest, NPCs talking with their mouth closed, identical NPCs spawning in the same place, cars crashing into each other and exploding when you're not looking at the road (sometimes it looked like one car spawned on top of another and exploded), V picking up the phone, saying she can't talk right now and then immediately calling the person back, and many, many more.

- I've seen a lot of people complaining about the game's poor performance, but in my case it wasn't that bad and mostly ran smoothly even though my computer isn't high-end. It randomly crashed twice and that's it. Perhaps I just got lucky.

Overall, I'd say it's a pretty fun game but it does have a lot of flaws and I definitely recommend buying it at a discount. Maybe if I didn't have such high expectations because so many people consider this game to be one of the best, I wouldn't be so critical.

Cyberpunk 2077 might have the greatest gaming comeback.

When the game launched, it was basically a bug simulator with some emotional damage included for free. Players were crashing more than their in-game cars, and CD Projekt Red got cooked by the entire internet.

But instead of giving up and disappearing into the shadows like a stealth build, the developers kept grinding. Update after update, they fixed bugs, improved gameplay systems, reworked mechanics, and finally delivered the experience people were originally hyped for. Then came Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, which honestly felt like the developers saying: “Alright, let us cook one more time.”

And somehow… they actually did.

Now Night City feels alive, polished, and insanely immersive. You can genuinely tell the devs cared about the game and refused to let it die. That kind of dedication is rare nowadays.

Cyberpunk 2077 went from being the internet’s favorite joke to one of the best RPG experiences of the last years and honestly, that redemption arc deserves respect.

Thank you CDPR, and never stop fighting.

I’m on my fifth playthrough now, and somehow Cyberpunk 2077 still feels more alive than most new open world games coming out today. Night City isn’t just a map, it feels like a real place with exhausted people, fake dreams, dirty money, and nonstop chaos hiding behind neon lights.

What surprised me the most after replaying it so many times is how emotional the game actually is. Under all the chrome, guns, and explosions, Cyberpunk is really about loneliness, identity, survival, and trying to matter before the world forgets you. Few games make side characters feel this human. Panam, Judy, Johnny, Viktor they genuinely feel like people you knew for a while instead of quest dispensers.

And honestly? The atmosphere is unmatched. Driving through Night City at 2 AM with the radio on while rain hits the windshield is still one of the hardest vibes gaming has ever created. No game captures “beautiful but broken” like this one.

People talked nonstop about the bad launch, but after five runs, I can confidently say the comeback deserves just as much attention. The amount of detail, storytelling, soundtrack, world building, and freedom in combat is insane now. Whether you play stealth, netrunner, samurai build, or complete cyberpsycho, the gameplay actually lets you feel unique.

The craziest part is that Cyberpunk doesn’t try to make you feel like a hero. It constantly reminds you that in Night City, almost everyone loses something. And that’s exactly why the story hits harder than most RPGs.

Five playthroughs later and I still catch small details I missed before. That’s rare. Most games get boring after one ending. Cyberpunk somehow gets more personal the longer you stay in Night City.

“Wrong city. Wrong people.”
Still one of the coldest lines in gaming.

That's an amazing and absolutely unforgettable game.

Cyberpunk 2077 is all about the process. You can spend a few hours in Night City and not even notice how much time has passed. You WANT to explore. Maybe it's just me, but I genuinely wanted to look into every district, discover every possible thing, and just live in that city for a while. Night City feels believable — and at some point, you stop feeling like a player and start feeling like a person living there.

This game has an insane amount of content. There’s always something to do. Gigs, side jobs, random encounters, characters, hidden stories — at times it feels endless. And honestly, trying to finish everything in one playthrough is almost impossible.

But then something interesting happens. When you finally start running out of things to do, the city begins to feel strangely empty. Almost confusing. Like, “come on… this is Night City, there should always be something happening.” And somehow, that feeling fits the game perfectly.

Of course, the game isn’t perfect. The biggest issue for me was the bugs. There are still plenty of them — sometimes small, sometimes really noticeable. Occasionally they can completely break the immersion and make you laugh at a serious moment. Maybe I’m just too used to Rockstar-level polish, but I definitely felt that Cyberpunk could’ve been more refined in terms of quality of the open-world details and overall gameplay interactions, not just "a beautiful picture".

And of course — the ending. The characters are written incredibly well, so whichever path you take, it hits hard. For me, this was a story about change. Everyone has their own V, their own journey, and their own version of Night City.

I definitely recommend this game to anyone who hasn't played it yet.

And for everyone who already finished their journey in Night City — a tight embrace 🫂

P.S. — whoever was responsible for the soundtrack deserves their hands kissed. Some tracks hit harder than entire missions.
