I will preface this review with the fact that I played and loved Witcher 3, so was expecting something along those lines, but more futuristic and of course with a new and different story.
Having seen the trailers and this being a new IP, I was excited, though knew from the start that I won't play on day one as I generally never do (for both monetary and bug reasons).
Turns out this could not have been a better idea, given the absolute shambles the game was in on launch.

After all of the bugs were sorted and the DLC was released, I finally decided to sink my teeth into the game, and when I say that, I mean it, as I have put in 230 hours into the game, finishing every main story mission as well as every side gig / side mission.
Given the amount of time I've spent, you would think that I was a big fan of the game, but sadly, Cyberpunk is no Witcher and the game ultimately disappointed me.
Without getting too into the weeds, the world just didn't pull me in, which mostly resulted from (in my opinion) poor writing, plot inconsistencies, characters that are not likeable and are either shoehorned in or are clearly missing something (presumably due to content being cut) and of course, the bugs.
Don't get me wrong, there are definitely parts where the game shines and some missions that were really impactful and well written, however all this was in a sea of inconsistencies and issues, which ultimately made me disinterested.
I started and stopped playing this game multiple times, but just kept pushing myself to go through everything and "experience" the game fully, but at the end I feel like most of it was a waste of time.

All in all, Cyberpunk is not a terrible game, but it is definitely very flawed.
While it is definitely a cultural moment in gaming history, it's remembered more for how it launched than for what it actually is. And that's the problem: strip away the redemption narrative and you're left with a good-looking game built on a shaky foundation. The highs are real, but they're rare, and they never added up to the experience I'd hoped for. I'm glad I finally played it, if only to form my own opinion - but I don't see myself going back, and I'd struggle to tell anyone they need to.

P.S. If you do end up playing it, the Phantom Liberty DLC is MANDATORY!

Cyberpunk 2077 — A Modern Masterpiece

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that feels less like a product and more like a fully realized artistic vision. Night City is not just a setting — it is a living, breathing organism, filled with ambition, decay, beauty, violence, and humanity. From the moment you step into its neon-soaked streets, the game pulls you into a world that feels both terrifyingly dystopian and strangely believable.

What impressed me most is how well Cyberpunk 2077 combines atmosphere, storytelling, character writing, exploration, and player choice. The main story is emotional, stylish, and deeply personal, but the side quests are often just as memorable. Many of them feel handcrafted, meaningful, and written with the kind of detail you rarely see in open-world games. The characters are outstanding, the dialogue is sharp, and the world constantly gives you reasons to care.

The gameplay has also become excellent. Combat is fast, flexible, and satisfying, whether you prefer hacking enemies from the shadows, going in with blades, using firearms, or building your own hybrid playstyle. The RPG systems, cyberware, weapons, and progression all make the experience feel rewarding from start to finish.

The DLC content only makes the game stronger. It adds more depth, more emotional weight, more style, and more reasons to return to Night City. Everything feels like it expands the world naturally rather than simply adding extra content for the sake of it.

Yes, the game had issues at launch. That is impossible to ignore. But judging Cyberpunk 2077 as it stands today, those early technical problems do not define the experience anymore. What remains is an incredible open-world RPG with unforgettable atmosphere, powerful storytelling, and one of the most immersive cities ever created in gaming.

For me, Cyberpunk 2077 is not just a great game. It is a masterpiece. A bold, emotional, visually stunning, and unforgettable experience that deserves to be remembered as one of the defining games of its generation.

This game is all over the place. In some instances it's fantastic, then it rips your heart out with how undercooked it is in other places and your immersion is quickly broken.

[h2]Story and narrative[/h2]
The premise of the world is simple - megacorpos run most of the world in a world where governments inexplicably bent over to them nearly everywhere regardless of the system, yet it fails to deliver that feeling in the most corpo-driven city. For some odd reason, their presence is visible everywhere, yet felt nearly nowhere throughout the story, even in quests where you are screwing with the corporations, and I blame the writing and pacing here. Edgerunner immediately pulls you into a world run by corpos, whereas the game tries it in so many ways, and still falls flat. This corpo narrative began and ended with Meredith Stout. That was a fantastic introduction to what corpos can and would do, and then it just fizzles out. They quickly became a background noise even though your whole main quest is related to dealing with them. Gangs became the focal point and the pacing prioritized them and the result is tangible.

Narrative is also suffering from pacing and writing. Just like in Fallout, you need to fulfill your mission before time runs out. Here however, it does not run out, because the world is filled with side quests and we wouldn't want to miss out on that. A terrible mistake. Cake-and-eat-it-too kind of a mistake. On top of that, you are bombarded with endless phonecalls in the very first hour of gameplay, to the point you begin to lose track of what certain quests or side characters are about and you do not know what to do first. How this wasn't ever patched or why it was introduced in the first place is beyond me.

The first mission is the best example of this dissonance. It's an endless stream of information and cutscenes that attempt to pull you into the story but they instead leave you dazed and confused. You're meeting over a dozen characters within your first hour, which is filled with cutscenes that inform you about three subsequent missions. Incomparable to the pacing of Witcher 3's beginning. Absurdly terrible but am I glad I stuck through it, as I knew what they were attempting to do.

[h2]World and immersion[/h2]
I don't think I've ever played a game so immersive and yet so shallow at the same time. Citizens are immersion-breaking, but then you get to live a second life within this world as long as you're not done with much of the story, but as you finish quests, immersing in it becomes less and less interesting to you. Why? Because CD Projekt Red is not Rockstar nor Valve. They've created a static world that tries to simulate a dynamic one. Compare the world to GTA's where the world is an actual, reactive sandbox. Everything is designed to react to a trigger - from the world, from the characters, from the physics. In Cyberpunk, you are the sole trigger, and the game reminds you of it every so often. In GTA5 you can't drink, car interiors are awful, apartments are lackluster and staticky, the interaction with the world objects is undercooked, CP77 builds on that in so many ways, but it just didn't have the funding, time and tech know-how to build a living world, and one feels and sees it.

The city itself is beautiful to look at. The more you explore though, the more you see the seams unfortunately, but it's well detailed. Not many interiors to enter, some interiors are only a one-time occurrence, some are notably undercooked.

[h2]Characters' reactivity[/h2]
It's a heavily narrative-driven game, relatively loose where it can afford to be, but otherwise you are shoehorned into a particular V every single time no matter your background. However, your choices do matter when it comes to characters you come across - their fate, and the reaction to your actions, are a direct consequence of your doing. They act in juxtaposition to certain choices you make throughout quests or stories, which allows you to really ponder on the eventual outcomes, though some outcomes will certainly leave you confused as to why X happened, and will feel forced as a consequence. Again, writing isn't the strongest suit of this game, pacing exacerbates it, but the characters are well fleshed out and they thankfully salvage the entire game. They suffer from a few things though - terribly animated vehicle cutscenes where they're the ones driving, mistimed voice lines and sound EQ being all over the place. The loud and annoying ads sometimes cut through very emotional lines so awfully, it left me extremely annoyed.

[h2]The technical slavjank nightmare[/h2]
No wonder why they decided to go for Unreal Engine 5. The accumulated tech debt became too great. They're not a large corporation yet still they built an amazing looking engine that does things it's set out to do relatively well. But it is indeed a pig with a lipstick in every way imaginable and you get reminded of it while playing quite often. I will not list them here.

[h2]Phantom Liberty DLC[/h2]
Very happy they eventually fixed most of the issues plaguing the game and even released a fantastic DLC. They doubled down on a game they worked their asses off for nearly a decade. The writing and pacing there is immeasurably better and it shows what CP77 could've been had they simplified the whole premise and focused on building a reactive world. Instead, they branched the main story out and the further you strayed from the beginning the more it suffered. This is a non-issue in the DLC. It's a relatively simple and arguably much more linear approach to an immersive and atmospheric story with memorable characters and, finally, very few side characters you're supposed to remember after a dozen or so quests. I still remember Paco and his friend I smuggled out of Dogtown, the chippery merchant who kept spamming me with tidbits about events that happened a week ago in game for some reason.

[h2]Modding![/h2]
Hell yeah. So many great mods that we will not get to use once the new installment is launched on UE5. Plenty of mods brought back cut content and fix bugs that are still present. Imho they are vital for those who really want a great experience, doubly so for replays.

This is a really, really good game.  I remember first downloading GOG over 10 years ago and that's all they would advertise:  "Cyberpunk 2077!"  I was like, "Great, another future title is being over-advertised and over-hyped.  It will probably end up sucking."  Well, I was half-right, because it did suck initially when it was released.  I figured I wouldn't even give it a chance because have little faith in developers with investors who rush and over-hype everything, like No Man's Sky, for example, but I was talking to a friend about Cyberpunk 2077 a year or so ago and he said the game has improved significantly.  So, I decided to get it.

No regrets.  I had a ton of fun playing and re-playing this game.  There are so many main quests and side quests that intermingle with the main quests and side quests that don't intermingle with the main quest, but intermingle with other side quests and independent side quests and gigs and crimes to resolve and races, etc.  There's so much content it was almost overwhelming, but in a good "I am getting my money's worth out of this game" way.

The story is pretty dystopian and bleak.  I'm pretty sure the developers don't really believe in "winners" as we do in a lot of games.  Decisions can be very difficult to make, unless your ambition is to get the most gain out of it.  However, if you're trying to be a "good" person, this game makes it difficult to do, because most story-driven choices have good and bad sides to them.  I won't spoil anything, but you'll see when you experience it.  And it's not just the main quest, there are side quests that have this same dynamic.  It was morally challenging.  My only problem was that, with each ending I discovered, I felt like I was finally making the right choice, but then the writers throw a random wrench into the ending that kind of ruins it for me.  I got a little tired of that, but like I said, this game wasn't meant to be good vs bad.

Ok, potential spoiler ahead, but I can't resist.  I recognized Keanu Reeves the moment I saw him.  I hadn't realized he was in this game, but he did a marvelous job in his role and he's a great actor.  I think a big part of this game's success is because of him.  I won't lie, though, I hated his character my first playthrough, and I wanted nothing to do with him.  However, the game slowly and surely makes him seem decent and enables you to understand things from his point of view.  He's still a bit of a jerk, but as I mentioned before, this game doesn't cater to your whim.

Oh yeah, I almost forgot, developers are finally recognizing and representing straight-edge and sexually-abstaining persons.  I was getting so tired of games ruining characters for me by having them get drunk, do a bunch of drugs and sleep around like degenerates without giving me the option to avoid it.  I was glad to finally have the choice to graciously decline alcohol, cigarettes, drugs, promiscuity, etc. if I wanted.  Speaking of such, you can turn off any and all nudity in this game.  Female characters will have a black, bra-like texture over their bosoms if they're "naked" and they'll be wearing panties.  Male characters will always have boxers on at least.  However, if you want the nudity, you can even change the size of your ding-dong or rack.  Aside from the cosmetic viewpoint, I don't think this mechanic adds anything else to the game.

So, weapons, cybernetic implants, clothing and outfits and consumables are numerous.  I found myself always discovering something new or better than what I had.  There's also a huge amount of "written" dialogue, in the form of data shards.  This can also be a little annoying, because I could either be sneaking around, fighting enemies and looting stashes and corpses, etc. and I'd pick up like 18 different data shards that I'd have to go to my journal to read.  Normally, that's not so bad if you can ignore it, but each data shard shows up as a bolded item under an extensive list of categories.  The "other" category being the biggest culprit because I'd have like 75 unread data shards in there because I'm not going to pause my game every 5 seconds to read shard number 54 of the 87 that I somehow got from the 5 gangsters I just hollowed out, neither am I going to analyze every stash I search for every little thing I want to pick up or not. Anyway, I'm happy to say that this game turned out great.  If you're looking for a new first-person action adventure, definitely play this.

I first bought this game on release. It was a terrible, broken mess. 

I tried the game again after 5 years, and it was a totally new game. Great job from CDPR to fix it. 

Some criticisms:

The game still has quite a few bugs, but most are harmless and sometimes funny. Not to be unexpected for a game this complex and big. However, considering the game's tone is serious, I do think it would be great to iron them out for the sake of preventing immersion breaks. 

Personally, I didn't like the English voice acting for male V nor female V. Perhaps just me, but it just felt a bit goofy, lacking in emotion, etc. They also reused quite a few voice lines and at times it is noticeable.

The game's pacing is also very awkward. There is quite a lot to do, except the game feels like it rushes you to complete the main storyline as you are dying in a matter of weeks. It seems like it was a big mistake to make that such a prominent part of the story so early on. It is also very difficult to care about Jackie, as you basically experience none of their previous relationship. I almost wonder if it was cut content. 

I won't get into the details, but the pacing of the main game was not good, and it also felt quite short. It would have been great to have some time being a regular merc with Jackie before everything begins to go downhill.

There are a ton of details that have not been attended to, and are only partially fixed by mods (reflection in mirrors, for example).

I think player customization is also quite limited, accessible building interiors are limited as well. As you get more cyberware, your character does not reflect it. A shame. 

Some random things that really came to bother me are how CDPR approached buildings that don't have accessible interiors. Instead of designing a model for the player to view from the window, they simply emplaced a 3D drawing that looks terrible if you look at it for longer than a second. And it is standardized, so you seem the same pattern everywhere, and it is quite immersion breaking. I wonder if they did it procedurally, because there are several spots on the map that you CAN actually go inside, but when viewing it from the outside window, it is just painted over with the same 3D drawing. This creates impossible physical dimensions and mismatched interiors/exteriors, etc.

Same thing with NPCs. Play long enough (just 10 hours was enough to notice), and you will realize that there are a limited number of base NPC models, of which all other NPCs are just variations of. Incredibly immersion breaking.

Your decisions in the game, as well as the life path you take in the game, basically do not matter except for the very end. That was quite frustrating. I also felt it was very limiting. If I wanted to roleplay as a diehard corpo, even after getting discarded, it is impossible to do so as your dialogue locks you into a certain philosophy and playstyle. 

The romantic options are generally all terrible. I didn't like any of the characters that you had an option to romance. Only Kerry was fine, and it just feels wrong to romance him while being half-Johnny. 

A lot of times, the dialogue prompts are completely different to what is actually said by V. Not just semantically different, directionally different. Very frustrating and a confusing design choice.

There is still a lot more to complain about, but those are the things that immediately come to mind.

Some compliments:

The graphics are generally great for a 2020 release. It is a visually stunning game. The atmosphere, overall story, and execution are well done. 

What really saves this game, in my opinion, is the Phantom Liberty DLC. What a fantastic addition. I think it is better than the base game by far. The story is dynamic, morally grey, your decisions have profound consequences, it just does everything you would like it to. The characters are well fleshed out, flawed, and make the story incredibly captivating. As much as I like Keanu Reeves, I think not having the DLC be as focused on Johnny allowed CDPR to make something really special. It's a spy thriller meeting the Cyberpunk world. It was truly awesome.

Replayability is also pretty decent. Combat is fun. The cyberware is fun. For the most part, especially if you are able to ignore details (I struggle a bit), the game is very immersive. 

I am really looking forward to Cyberpunk 2 (Orion), and I hope that not having to focus on Johnny will allow them to really flesh out a great story.

To be fair, it's still not perfect, and you will definitely run into some annoying bugs and glitches from time to time. But despite these flaws, the incredible atmosphere and emotional story make it completely worth your time. It’s a solid 8/10 that you shouldn't miss.

[h3]A generational game, but not without flaws[/h3]

To preface this review: my only experience with any souls-like was 'The First Berserker: Khazan', and I never finished it.
Actually, I almost never finished Elden Ring either. A few hours in, and I was ready to quit, but the sheer number of players glazing this game was bugging me. "What do they see, that i dont?''
I couldn't tell you exactly when I found my answer; it was more of a gradual experience. But I do now understand, even if I don't fully agree.

The [b][i]world[/i][/b] that's built here is amazing. The ambience and overall vibes made me feel like this was a living, breathing realm full of despair and danger. Even without many cut scenes, I could still grasp the severity and gravity of the events that had taken place. (even if most of the time i had no idea what was happening in the story)

The [b][i]combat[/i][/b], while at times was a little frustrating, is still one of its best features. The build diversity and scope are something special that I can't really find a comparison to in anything else I've played before it. 
The bosses, too, were imaginative and challenging, and more than a few times I found myself jumping out of my seat and slamming my desk in excitement after I defeated them.

There's more I could praise, but I won't, because so many reviews have already done that. So instead ill bring up a few of the [b][i]negatives[/i][/b] that i dont see mentioned very often.
The target locking in this game is dreadful. I swear I died more times to this than actual bosses. It's mostly fine when you have a single enemy to deal with, but as soon as there are multiple targets, it fails miserably.
The other massive flaw I feel this game has is with its in-game systems/mechanics. I can't think of a single game I've ever played that required me to tab out and Google as many times as this. It really was ridiculous. There is just so much that isn't explained or explained well, and most players will miss out on a lot of content or waste a lot of time without Alt-tabbing and turning to guides. 

Overall though, I'm happy I put the time in and finished it. It was a great adventure.

Elden Ring took everything that made Dark Souls great, dialled it up a bunch of notches, and set you loose in an open world.

I wasn't initially sold on the idea of an Open world souls game, but I can honestly say that I think it was a fantastic move to make the genre accessible to new players. Far more so than in the souls series, if you hit a wall you can often pick another direction very easily, find new dungeons or encounters, and hunt for loot and runes without specifically banging your head against a wall. Pair this with the spirit ashes allowing summons in almost every boss fight that you can level with you, and this is a great starting point for newcomers to the genre.

If you're a veteran, the game has you covered too, since there's no NEED to engage with summons if you don't want to. The fights escalate a lot as the game goes on, and really make you feel rewarded for learning the dances in a way I feel is only beaten by Sekiro in the Genre.

The premise of Elden Ring was really quite simple. You know this iconic series of challenging action games FromSoftware is known to make? Take that and make it bigger, grander and epic. Make it Dark Souls, but open world. Then give GRR Martin yet another excuse not to finish the Winds of Winter by hiring him to create for you a backstory full of weird incestuous genderfluid gods. Finally, add to the mix a strange horse-goat of a mount and you have something really quite unusual. That's the premise and the promise. Now whether it delivers on that promise or not that's a different discussion. One that after spending a good 200 hours on this game's expansive world, perhaps I can answer.

Let's begin with the elephant in the room. The open world. This is one damn big elephant, truly ginormous. It goes on and on. Mountains, swamps, frozen over lakes, caverns, vast underground locations. This is one of the bigger games I have played and it's filled with details. It's also terrifyingly beautiful. The rich use of colour, the stunning landscapes, the dramatic vistas, the incredible heights. The game's art direction is top-notch. I would argue it's era defining. However there is an important caveat to consider. The open world is an incredible achievement yes, but how well does it serve the game's other mechanics.

Here the picture becomes somewhat less celebratory. You see the game retains its Dark Souls bones, the nuanced, environmental story-telling, the sparse quests driven by occasional meetups. Only now this spans a vastly larger surface and becomes a lot harder to experience naturally. Put simply, a great number of quests are next to impossible to do correctly without a guide. Not because of the minimalist design and lack of compasses, but exactly because of how incongruous the quest design is when applied to an open world. You execute a step in a quest. The character moves. Where? Go figure. In Dark Souls progression was linear and this was not much of an issue. Here, it is.

On gameplay this is largely Dark Souls still. Except significantly easier. This is likely another side-effect of the open world direction. I'm not saying the game is not challenging. Rush ahead and you will be punished. However, the game rewards careful exploration, as it rewards skilful combat. Generously. And there is plenty of rewarding side-content to conquer. Do that enough and by the endgame even superbosses won't be that scary. On a smaller scale, a disappointing element was the complete lack of a swimming ability. So many inviting islands close to the coast that are impossible to reach without gimmicks. The moment your character reaches the darker shade of waters down they go, as if they reached the proverbial end of the world. Be that as it may, this is a competently made and entertaining action game. Given its pedigree, I would expect no less.

Technically speaking the game is less impressive than its stellar art direction might suggest. Its graphical prowess in particular is decent but not extraordinary. There are sloppy technical decisions present that I wouldn't expect to see in a modern game. For example the lack of ultra wide monitor support. Even Dark Souls Remastered had that. But not Elden Ring? What's worse, the game is taking anti-cheating a bit too seriously and attempting to mod the game to include missing functionality can mark you as a cheater. I ended up having to play the game completely offline and with the use of extraneous software that didn't integrate quite seamlessly enough. All so that I could make the game work properly with my setup. FromSoftware really needs to do better here.

To conclude, does Elden Ring deliver on its promise. Is this Dark Souls but open world and is that a good thing? The first question is easy. Yes, it definitely is. The minimalist story telling, the challenging combat, the well crafted world. It's all here. The second question is harder. Dark Souls is not an open world game and making it one required changes that occasionally felt like discounts to the formula. In the end this is a lovingly made game of incredible ambition. It is beautiful and it is flawed. Is it worth playing? Absolutely, it's also worth pondering. There is something truly monumental just a few improvements away.

Elden Ring is one of the most impressive open-world RPGs ever made. Developed by FromSoftware and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game combines the challenging combat the studio is known for with a massive world full of exploration, secrets, and unforgettable encounters.

The Lands Between is a stunning setting that constantly rewards curiosity. Every region feels unique, from haunting castles to underground cities hidden beneath the world. Unlike many open-world games, exploration rarely feels repetitive because there is always something interesting around the next corner.

Combat is deep and satisfying, offering a huge variety of weapons, spells, and character builds. Boss battles are a major highlight, requiring skill, patience, and strategy. While the difficulty can be intimidating for newcomers, the game's open structure allows players to explore elsewhere and grow stronger before tackling tougher challenges.

The story is mysterious and often told through environmental details, item descriptions, and character interactions. This approach won't appeal to everyone, but it creates a sense of discovery that fits the game's world perfectly.

The few drawbacks include occasional performance issues and a lack of traditional quest tracking, which can sometimes leave players confused about where to go next. However, these flaws are minor compared to the overall experience.

Overall, Elden Ring is a masterpiece that successfully blends challenging gameplay, rewarding exploration, and rich world-building. Whether you're a longtime fan of FromSoftware games or a newcomer looking for an unforgettable adventure, it is a game well worth playing.

The best way I can describe this game is it is a bad GREAT game. There is no doubt that the game is great, however as far as great games go, I think this one is bad at it.

Starting with the negatives, the main one for me is just boss repeats. I don't want to fight 3 Margit's or 5 Demi-Human's or whatever. So there are somewhere around 200 bosses I think? But maybe only about 50 of them are unique? And I understand that you can't really have a game with over 200 unique bosses, but I just find it quite lazy and honestly a bit of a turn off. Why are there 2 Godrick's or 3 Morgott fights or whatever, to me it just doesn't make sense and where yeah, you get more overall boss fight time (which is the fun of the souls games) repeating it in this way? No fun.

Another issue I have is the game feels more like a dodge simulator, some bosses feel like they give you no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ room to attack. It takes me back to DS3 Pontiff where you just never get a damn turn and honestly, I hate that. I'm not saying I want 5 second long openings to get free staggers, but I don't want to have to do 8 dodges, 1 attack, another 6 dodges, 1 attack, but I also don't want to have to trade damage just because I want to attack. I think some bosses aren't balanced well at all for this, and I think the DLC makes it more of a prominent issue.

That said, that's the main negatives for me, a couple small gripes could also be things like I don't find the Catacombs fun, just felt lengthy imo, I didn't really like the whole underground in Siofra, the area was just a bit tedious, and I do wish you could navigate the map a bit faster especially in NG+, going for graces again takes so long. Add a Surge Sprint into this just like Nightreign, would honestly help so much.

All that said, I still think it's a great game. There really is an endless amount of things to do. And one thing I really love is the weapon variety. In Dark Souls, it felt like you could just get a Uchigatana and be set, but in this I actually wanted to try new weapons. Godskin Peeler with Black Flame Tornado was so much fun for me, then things like the Fallingstar Beast Jaw also has such a cool and unique skill to it, I do love the variety in that and love how almost all weapons feel useable. And then there's magic to swap things up even more, even though I think melee is way more fun, the spells were cool and you could get creative. 

Back to bosses, for what fights are actually unique, I think they are great. Some bosses are just obnoxious, like Red Wolf just running away and spamming Glintblades, it does get infuriating but every game is gonna have annoying bosses like that. I think pretty much all Great Rune bosses are cool, I love the final boss, love Radagon, love Godfrey, they are some very enjoyable bosses. 

Overall great game, definitely has potential to be a great great game, but for me the negatives of it really do take it down quite a bit, but that said the game itself is so good that I would still recommend it 100%.

Elden Ring is, in my opinion, the greatest video game ever made. It takes everything that made FromSoftware's previous games special and expands it into a massive open world filled with mystery, challenge, and unforgettable moments.

The world of the Lands Between is breathtaking. Every region feels unique, with stunning landscapes, hidden secrets, and incredible bosses waiting around every corner. Exploration is constantly rewarding because you never know what you'll discover next, whether it's a powerful weapon, a secret dungeon, or an entirely new area. Critics widely praised the game's open-world design, combat, and sense of discovery.

Combat is one of Elden Ring's strongest features. Every victory feels earned, and the variety of weapons, spells, and builds allows players to create their own unique playstyle. The boss fights are challenging, memorable, and some of the best in gaming history. Reviewers frequently highlighted the depth of the combat system and the creativity of its encounters.

The game's lore and atmosphere are equally impressive. Instead of telling its story through long cutscenes, Elden Ring encourages players to piece together its world through exploration and discovery. This makes the adventure feel personal and rewarding.

While the game can be difficult and occasionally overwhelming for newcomers, those willing to learn its systems will find one of the most rewarding experiences gaming has to offer. Its combination of exploration, combat, world-building, and freedom creates an adventure unlike any other.

Rating: 10/10

This game is basically LOTR, but if it was a videogame. 

This game deserves all of its flowers, and I want to add my piece: Limgrave is probably the smartest ease-in to an open-world I've ever come across. As soon as you leave the tutorial area, you open those doors, and the beauty of this game immediately leaves you in awe. You take your first steps toward whom you perceive as the welcome mat to this stunning spectacle, and get called maidenless. You see a Golden-armored horseman and are immediately filled with the determination to kill it, only to be stomped on like a bug. You can't seemingly fight him as you are now, unless you're willing to keep bashing your head at it, so you go on to explore. You look around and fight some enemies, only for them to kill you over and over again, and suddenly you're met with an exhaustion to put down the controller. You wake up the next day realize that whether its exploring or fighting a boss, there's no way you're going to progress unless you practice, so you take it slow and sneak up on a few enemies instead of taking them head on. you find a cool weapon and figure out how to start leveling up, and that same boss becomes trivial. That is the philosophy that is drilled into your head not even 30 minutes into the game, and yet it spans across your entire playthrough. you don't HAVE to explore every nook and cranny of the surrounding area until you level up enough to beat a boss easily, and you don't HAVE to die 40+ times until you kill a boss. That's what the game is telling you, the way you want to play is how the game is played. You can choose an int build and melt enemies with your magic. You can pick up the biggest sword you can find and make bosses to buckle easily, it's all up to you. 

I haven't completed the game more than once, but I will say I have played through at least Limgrave a few times a least. It's just that good. I would take the time to talk about the masterful level-design of Limgrave ALONE from a game-development perspective, but it would just turn into a full blown essay. Go play this game, its definitely more of a full package than any other game at it's pricing, and I've heard the DLC is its own full game, which is insane. First off, Elden Ring is not a bad game. The boss fights, visuals and world building are all cool, and while I finished the game and then some, its just... a drag. 

The world is massive, and you can really feel it. Exploration is a key to Elden Ring, and that can be fun at times. What is not fun, is the absurd scale of the game combined with a complete lack of non-filler content. Useless crafting materials, random ashes (another whole topic on its own) and grave glovewort being treated like "rewards" for exploring far off corners of the world, same one enemies in every dungeon, and half of the boss fights being "what if we did it again... but now there's two of them". Same one tree sentinel. Same one tree spirit.

With enemies scattered all over with nothing to gain from killing them, the game heavily encourages you to not fight, and just explore in the open world. What's that? John Knight patroling a random road drops a unique item, but you ignored him as he's literally a generic enemy found all over elsewhere? Oh well, thats unfortunate. Better luck next time. 

Souls games inherently will never be possible to mostly complete on a first run without some sort of guide, and quest chains even more so as they're intended to be done over multiple playthroughs, but the insane amount of NOTHING in this game that is just recycled over and over and over that you CANNOT skip without a guide because guess what, that one dungeon you chose to skip, missed or forgot was the one dungeon that didnt just have useless ashes in them. That one hill over there might have a key item for your build or quest chain, so you better go explore it thoroughly, but wait... there was nothing. Again.

As I started with, the game isnt bad. The game is mostly enjoyable. It has some crazy fights, its weapons and various forms of incantations/sorceries are very cool, but there's just too much in this game that has no place, or is recycled adding nothing but filler, for me to reccomend it before literally any other fromsoft souls game. If part of the enjoyment in these games for you is trying to explore and find as much as possible without help, the world is filled with far too much nothing, but hey, at least it will look pretty and the main boss fights will be cool.

I don't like FromSoftware games, I find them boring, they are often annoying and just suck. It is not hard to call them overrated, they are extremely popular and also quite edgy, and like in every other media, edgy titles tend to produce the most overrated works.

The problem, however, is in the small recurring things. Annoying sequences that have become FromSoftware signatures, despite being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Poison lakes with speed debuffs, terrible platform sections in an engine that clearly is not for that. Vague quest system that no longer works in an open world. Lingering AOEs (poison mists and fires) that you can't really roll through due to their size, despite the game being designed around roll. Bosses that keep repositioning after attacks (I played melee, ♥♥♥♥ Maliketh). Giant bosses that really don't work when you can't see them whole on camera. Some bosses just being recycled too much, like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dragons, I HATE GENERIC DRAGONS. Horse combat was ♥♥♥♥, but what game does vehicle combat well...

It's a good game, quite inconsistent, but you should play it.

As someone who's played Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, and Sekiro, Elden Ring is a bit of a mixed bag for me.

The biggest difference is obviously the open world. In the older games, if I got stuck on a boss, that boss became my entire problem. There weren't a hundred other places to go or things to do. The only option was to learn the fight and beat it. I really liked that feeling of being forced to overcome the obstacle in front of me.

With Elden Ring, I sometimes end up overwhelmed by all the choices. Even on my third playthrough of the base game (my first two were on Xbox), I still find myself wondering where I should go next or if there's something else I should be doing instead. The freedom is impressive, but it can also make the experience feel less focused.

That being said, everything else about the game is incredible. The combat, bosses, build variety, world design, music, and sense of discovery are all top-tier.

I still prefer the more linear design of Dark Souls and Sekiro, but that's really just personal preference. Other than the open-world structure not being my favorite, Elden Ring is a 10/10 game and easily one of the best games I've ever played.

terraria, oh where do i even start...

At first glance, Terraria looks like “2D Minecraft,” but that comparison honestly doesn’t do it justice. The game evolves from chopping trees and building tiny wooden houses into fighting screen-filling gods, exploring corrupted biomes, crafting hundreds of weapons, and slowly becoming an unstoppable force of destruction. The progression system is insanely satisfying because every boss unlocks new materials, stronger gear, harder enemies, and completely changes how the game feels.

The exploration is phenomenal too. Every world feels alive with hidden caves, floating islands, underground jungles, deserts, oceans, temples, corruption/crimson biomes, and secrets buried literally everywhere. The “just one more cave” effect is dangerously real. I’ve lost hours mining because I kept finding something new.

The boss design is another massive highlight. Early bosses feel manageable, but later fights become absolute chaos in the best way possible. Dodging lasers, explosions, flying swords, and giant eldritch horrors while your screen turns into a fireworks show never stops being exciting.The soundtrack deserves praise too. Some tracks are weirdly relaxing while others perfectly capture the tension of boss fights and dangerous biomes. The music becomes surprisingly nostalgic after enough hours.

Multiplayer makes everything even better. Building giant bases with friends, preparing arenas for bosses, and accidentally summoning something horrific before everyone is ready creates some of the funniest gaming moments imaginable.

At this point, Terraria feels less like a game and more like a massive adventure sandbox that somehow keeps rewarding curiosity no matter how long you play.

Terraria sits comfortably in my top 3 games of all time, and I don't say that lightly. I've put more hours into it than I care to admit.
On the surface it looks like a simple 2d minecraft. It is absolutely not that. It's a massive action adventure with hundreds of enemies, 20+ bosses, four character classes, and a progression system so well paced that you never really feel like you're grinding, you're just playing. Defeating a boss unlocks new materials, new characters show up in your town, and the world shifts around you. Then hardmode kicks in and essentially hands you a second game.
The building is great if that's your thing, the combat is genuinely satisfying, and playing with friends is some of the most fun I've had in co-op. But the thing that keeps me coming back is that feeling of not quite knowing what's around the next corner.
For the price, nothing comes close to the amount of content you get. Re-Logic has been updating this game for over a decade, for free, because they actually care about it. That shows.
You can also use Tmodloader, kind of obvious what it does, since it literally sayd mod in the name. It's the best mod application i've ever used for a game. it's smooth and easy to use. The base game is already so good and has so much content that you don't even need mods to be honest. 
If you haven't bought it yet, just do it. It's one of those games you'll still be thinking about long after you've put it down.

Exploring this game as a product of its time and as a milestone of gaming history, it's an interesting experience.

From a modern perspective, and when looking for something fun to play with friends, it's not worth it, and Terraria has been outclassed so severely by its successors that it's not something 

Many aspects of the game pad out its runtime, keeping players busy with mindless work to distract from the lack of content in what is essentially a boss rush game with optional base building stock full of debatably aesthetic choices. 

Modern games that are creating social and creative spaces have figured out that constantly respawning unthreatening enemies padding the game time without adding anything of value are not satisfying either type of player engaging with the game. For people that want to make progress, the event is unrewarding noise, and for the builders and decorators, it's an impediment to creativity.

The events are so samey that the pattern quickly gets grating; if it's a "Pirate Attack", a "Martian Invasion", or a "Blood Moon", it all plays out the exact same way with copy pasted mobs, loot tables, and tons of uninteresting gear offering no choices but the illusion of content. At times the game spawned "quirky" events back to back for hours. The developers have added an endgame item to skip the noisy mess, showcasing that even they don't think it's worthwhile to have them around, but padding.

Combining the above design issues with the outdated controls, graphics, and repetitive shrill noises in a poorly sound-balanced world and its persistent multiplayer issues where connecting to the server fails half the time the game and requires a restart, the game can be rather taxing for what ultimately amounts to a flat 40-hour experience with little care given to a post-endgame experience over the years. 
Being a very "Wiki-forward" experience, with most mechanics hidden from the player, from item stats to basic mechanics, the game expects you to play it while looking things up more so than modern titles.

Overall Impression

Hollow knight is a 2D Metroidvania that I didn’t think much of in the year 2026 considering where gaming is today. I was completely wrong. This game I felt was so simple has become one of my all-time favorite games.

Gameplay ★ ★ ★ ★ ★

Hollow Knight is very expansive game. Large map and a plethora of abilities to unlock. It also doesn’t hold your hand much so you’re left to discover and roam around the map. At times I was lost and I learned to make use of my map and mark things or points to come back to. I also love the combat. I am biased as souls-like is my favorite genre and this game brings a lot of it. From enemies to bosses I found my share of difficulty.

Story ★ ★ ★ 

I feel as though most souls-like lack a direct story most times and are somewhat ambiguous. Though I get the general story the lore is much more rich as to why everything is happening. I watched a YouTube vid that gave me more of an understanding and much more appreciation and intrigue to the story of Hallownest. Unfortunately without the lore hunters I don’t feel as though I’d understand as much of what’s going on just from my own playthrough.

Graphics/Visual Style/Audio ★ ★ ★ ★ ★

Though this is a 2D game I didn’t think I could appreciate as much as I did the art. Each biome felt like a completely different land and all of the interactions and art all fit within the theme of each biome. Very immersive. I would say the audio was decent and not too much to write home (I’m not really an audiophile) about other than it was good and matched most of the biomes and bosses that I’d fight.

Performance ★ ★ ★ ★ ★

Game is optimized well with no bugs to mention in my playthrough. I played the whole game using a controller. Very intuitive controls. Good UI that’s easy to navigate. 

Length/Replayability/Value ★ ★ ★ ★ ★

The game is decently long as I got lost and there’s some difficulty while learning bosses. It took me around 20hrs or so to beat the first time. There’s a lot of replayability if you’re an achievement hunter like me. And especially the Godhome expansion where it challenges you more and more through an intense gauntlet. Insane value for the price considering I have over 100hrs.

Pros/Cons

I feel as though the pros and cons can be on the same list for many but for me personally I enjoy the combat, exploration, immersion, biomes and map, and rich lore.

Final Verdict ★ ★ ★ ★ ★

Hollow Knight is a side-scrolling adventure game built around exploration and movement through connected areas. The visual style is hand-drawn and detailed, with a dark tone that gives each region a distinct identity. 

There is very little direct instruction on where to go, so progress mainly comes from paying attention to surroundings and slowly learning how different paths connect. At first it can feel unclear, but over time the layout starts to make more sense as new routes open after gaining movement abilities.

Movement between areas often requires returning to earlier places once new skills are obtained, which changes how older sections are viewed. Each region has its own map structure that has to be uncovered step by step, and locating mapping points becomes important for keeping track of routes. 

The combat is based on timing and positioning rather than simple attacks, with enemies following different patterns that require adjustment in approach. It is a highly engaging experience that rewards patience and exploration, and is a strong choice for those who like interconnected world design and skill-based progression.

I played the game using keyboard and mouse despite having an Xbox controller, because I personally prefer keyboard and mouse controls, even though I assume most players would choose a controller. To check and set up the keyboard and mouse binds, a screenshot of the layout is attached below as a reference for keyboard and mouse players.

Overall, the game offers a large world with many hidden routes, optional paths, and multiple possible outcomes based on how much is discovered. The control system works well and allows precise movement during both platform sections and battles. It stands out as a well-crafted experience with attention to detail and steady exploration throughout the entire journey from start to finish.

Hollow Knight is one of those rare games that completely pulled me in from start to finish. At first, I thought it was just another indie platformer, but the deeper I explored Hallownest, the more I realized how much care and passion went into every part of the game. The world feels alive despite being a fallen kingdom, with beautiful environments, memorable characters, and an atmosphere that constantly makes you want to see what's around the next corner.

The exploration is incredibly rewarding because the game doesn't hold your hand. Every new area feels like a genuine discovery, and finding hidden paths or secrets always gave me a sense of accomplishment. The combat is simple but satisfying, and the boss fights are some of the best I've experienced in a Metroidvania game. Many of them took me multiple attempts, but defeating them never felt unfair—it felt earned.

The soundtrack deserves special praise as well. It perfectly matches the mood of each area and made many moments even more memorable. While the game can be challenging and sometimes leaves you feeling lost, that's also part of what makes the adventure so special.

If you enjoy exploration, challenging combat, and games that trust players to figure things out on their own, Hollow Knight is an easy recommendation. It's easily one of the best indie games I've ever played and absolutely worth every hour I spent in it.

[SPOILER-FREE REVIEW]

Hollow Knight is an insane masterpiece, from its design to its code. When I first hopped in, I barely had any idea what to expect. After playing and nabbing all 63 achievements, I can confirm that this game itself was its own achievement. How it pushes the player and enhances their skill and coordination is what made it stand out to me. I'll be using this review to share my experience in Hallownest and why you should accept the invitation down into the void, too.

What first appeals to the eye with this game has to be the atmosphere. For an indie game made by a small team, the art is way ahead of its time. Depending on where you go, it blends with the whole scene and gives you an accurate mood of what the heck I'm about to see. Following off the atmosphere, the music is absolutely astonishing. From a faint violin to a dramatic orchestra, Mr. Larkin sure knows how to set the tone for the world and the battles.

Now, let's talk about the battles. You're a tiny, insignificant "insect" who wields a nail pried off your father's carpentry build, going against enemies five times your size. From a big mosquito devouring a pest, to an energetic rolly-polly-ahh red beetle living in the sewers. Each enemy and battle provides a unique experience, challenging you to learn off their movesets and your mistakes, and parrying them with a strategized comeback. Every encounter will be different, and it is up to you how you will follow through.

Best of all, the story. There may seem to be no book whatsoever in such barren caverns, but when you begin to give life to the quiet, the lost pages are found and the lore goes far deeper. Why are we here? Why does this character look familiar? Why are we drinking orange juice? When you uncover the truth, it may be too late to revert the changes... but that's why you're here - to resume the journey as the Hollow Knight.

But the story is not all. The wind's the limit where many secrets and collectibles can be uncovered. Discover remnants of Hallownest, or unlock useful/why-do-I-need-this thingamajigs. Take on different challenges and brush off a lost fragment of memories. How you wish to tell the tale is based off what you can find and what you can master.

Overall, I highly recommend playing Hollow Knight or watching the gameplay yourself. Either way, you will go through an incredible journey. A little adventurer, only learning that ambition costs them. A lot. You might feel strong, but your strength isn't just for battling. It's for the unexpected. If you hatched from your egg, where will you traverse? How are you going to hold that burden? Is it worth it?

My answers? Yes, yes, and... ... ... nah, I'm just messing with you. That little knight shows no expression whatsoever - it's born to kill. Go on out there and slaughter everything in sight!

If you're wondering whether you should try this game in 2026, the answer is probably yes. It's a great game, and it deserves all the praise it receives. That said, there are some annoying aspects of the game.

The movement is incredibly tight, and I always felt like it was my fault when I died - there's no annoying hitboxes or anything (in fact, I found the hitboxes pretty generous). All of the bosses, I think, are fantastic. They never felt unfair to me. The artstyle and atmosphere is wonderful. Within an area, different rooms could look pretty similar/repetitive, but each area had a really distinctive feel. I knew when I had circled back to an area just by the changes in environment. I had no interest in the lore, but I attribute that to personal preference since there seems to be plenty of item descriptions and secrets to sink your teeth into.

I had a couple gripes with some QoL things. Why, for instance, do I have to waste charm slots to see my location on the map? Why do I have to waste slots on having my currency collected for me? I don't feel like these things really add to the game or the experience, they're just arbitrary restrictions on charms. And why bother with the Shade after you die? It's not really a challenge to fight it, more annoying than anything else. Last thing I'll say is that some of the foreground and background artwork made it hard to see what I was doing. It was at its worst in Deepnest, and I don't know if that's intentional or not.

All in all, a really great game. Absolutely worth a play if you're into Metroidvanias, Soulslikes, or if you're just curious. The entire experience is really memorable, especially some of the side content. If you go into it having already come to terms with a couple of the annoying parts, I think you'll have a great time. Also, the Path of Pain is so hilariously difficult, I had a really great time with that. Almost like the devs were having a laugh.

When I first started playing Hollow Knight, I was very bad at it.

Very. Bad.

However, this did not deter me, and little by little I continued onward throughout the game, slowly getting better at the platforming, at the combat, the fact that it was  metrovania, a game genre I didn't know existed, I had just heard good things about it and wanted to try something I'd never tried before.

While traveling through the world, I discovered a bug being eaten by an enormous, flying creature. I knew I had to save him, so after far too many tries, I saved him... I saved Zote. I expected gratitude, a thank you, or perhaps some cocky wanna be hero telling me he had it under control... I got the last one, but it was... ruder than I ever could have imagined... insulting, degrading, just a horrible, horrible bug... yet, I was fond of this horrible little creature. "Perhaps I'll encounter him again, and I'll be able to help him change into a better bug on my journey!" I thought to myself, and happily continued on my way, happy to have saved a life.

Some time later, and after much more improvement, I found a hidden passage way in the Fungal wastes, and within it, at the top of what at the time was a very difficult platforming challenge for me, I saw a lost, scared, bug, clearly on the verge of being taken by the infection. I kept trying, and trying, and trying to traverse this not even difficult challenge, determined to save this bug, whoever they were, and return them to safety, and eventually, I did... I saved Bretta.

Instantly I fell in love with Bretta (not romantically of course), she was so sweet, so shy, so lost, feeling completely and utterly forgotten, yet here I was, and I was now her only friend.

Continuing on with my travels, I would frequently stop into Dirtmouth, and would always check on Bretta, for I didn't want her to feel alone, nor forgotten. Her infatuation with Ghost was honestly endearing to me, for she was never weird about it, she was never obsessive, nor odd, she was just shy, sweet, and quiet, even when her diary entries offered a completely different side of her. Even if her stories were exaggerated, even if they weren't real, I always looked forward to reading the next entry, for it was nice seeing someone so real within that small town. Dare I think it, I wanted to be the white knight she saw me as. Visiting Bretta became a wonderful tradition for me, and sitting beside her on the bench gave me a huge sense of connection to the world, a reason to always come back to Dirtmouth.

Then I went into Deepnest.

There, I once again discovered Zote in peril, and once again I rushed in to save him, hoping that perhaps this time he'd show a bit of character growth, or even a half baked attempt at a thank you. I did not receive this, I instead received insults, degradation, and rudeness. Still though, I just rolled my eyes, and thought to myself, "Oh Zote, when will you learn?" Thus, I continued on, happy to have saved a life again.

Much later, once I was in the Colosseum of Fools, I once again found Zote, though this time locked in a cage, with once again nothing but insults to offer me. I laughed to myself, wished him luck, and entered the Challenge of the Warrior. I was mortified when at the end a huge, shaking cage dropped from above, only to burst into laughter when Zote appeared, waving his wooden sword pathetically and tripping on his own feet. Reluctantly, for I was worried I'd kill him, I did fight him, and sent him flying, sticking him in the ground by his own horns.

"Oh Zote," I thought to myself, "when will you learn?" Thus, I continued on with my journeys, wondering when Zote would change...

Then I got back to Dirtmouth.

I expected to see Bretta sitting on the bench, or perhaps sleeping in her room, a new diary entry ready to be read, a new story about her white knight just waiting to be seen. I was so looking forward to seeing her again, it truly had been a long time, and I looked forward to our silent time together...

What did I find?

ZOTE.

I found ZOTE, rambling on so loudly that the whole town could hear it, with Bretta... My dear, sweet, shy Bretta, blushing, listening to his monstrous, horrible, inflated lies, completely and utterly enamored.

My world went black.

Instantly I rushed into her room, only to find it had been overtaken by ZOTE. ZOTE not filled her journal, while any mentions of me were dashed to pieces by this horrible creatures lies, framing me as a cowardly villain within his own story. Images of ZOTE now filled her walls, the plushy of Ghost now replaced with something far more grotesque, more annoying, more... ZOTE.

Just when all hope seemed lost, I then found it... a basement within Bretta's home... which held a great, paper mache stature of ZOTE with dream particles coming off of it.

This was it, if I could beat this, I could rid myself of ZOTE.

I quickly entered the battle, needle drawn and ready, prepared to face on whatever horrors awaited me...

Or so I thought...

I wasn't expecting to see Bretta atop a bed, being fanned and served by ZOTE'S... nor did I expect the GREY PRINCE ZOTE.

I'll not go into detail, I simply cannot describe it, truly, it was... grotesque.

However, in the end I vanquished the enemy, and upon emerging victorious, I quickly ran back to find Bretta, ready to hear her tell off Zote, to kick him out of the town, to find herself and her confidence!

Instead, she now looked rather uninfatuated, bored even, with her once Grey Prince. Liking what I saw, but confused all the same, I returned to the basement, only to find that the dream particles were still there. Knowing what I had to do, I returned into that wretched abyss, ready to fight him however many times I needed to to win her back. I battled against ZOTE four times, each battle becoming more and more unfathomable, truly, grotesque in every way imaginable.

When I earned my fourth victory, I emerged, hoping to find my Bretta, hoping to discover ZOTE gone, or being told off, something, anything!

What I found instead shattered me to my very core.

I found Bretta gone, and Zote still rambling on loudly to no one at all.

Panicked, I searched her diary for answers, and to my horror discovered that she had indeed awakened from ZOTE'S spell... and left Hollownest entirely because of it in order to truly find herself.

Gone.

My dear, sweet, shy Bretta was gone...

NOW REPLACED WITH ZOTE!!!!!!!!

I did everything I could to make him leave, I listened to all his precepts, I fought his dream form until I simply couldn't do it anymore, I did EVERYTHING!!!

But he just wouldn't leave.

I was stuck with him, rambling for the whole town to hear, for the rest of my playthrough...

While Bretta was gone forever.

I was heartbroken.

...

I've since started my second playthrough, and once again found myself staring up at ZOTE, being chewed on by that great, wonderful vengefly. I could have saved him, I'm better now, it wouldn't have been a problem, I'm a great player. 

Why on earth would I do that though, when I can keep Bretta safe in Dirtmouth, and perhaps more importantly, safe from ZOTE? When I can keep Dirtmouth safe from ZOTE?

Ladies and gentlemen, non-binary friends, do you know why you should play Hollow Knight? The real reason you should play Hollow Knight?

It's so that you can get the NEGLECT achievement, and truly, truly, keep Dirtmouth, and Hollownest for that matter as well as all it's inhabitants safe from that horrible, rude, insulting, lying, terrible, monstrous, ugly, belittling, manipulating, stupid, rambling, annoying, insidious bug known as ZOTE.

Thank you for your time.

First of all, GLaDOS will be forever my hear me out.

If Portal was an apetizer, than Portal 2 is for sure a main course.
I do believe that it is nearly a perfect continuation. The only thing arguably wrong could be the fact that Portal had a constant feeling of isolation and horror, while Portal 2 doesn't feel that way - it has elements of it, obviously, but it's more of a storytelling comedy. I think it is because of the coop experience - how could you smoothly make a transition between horror main story and silly coop? You couldn't and that is why Portal 2 is more of a comedy.

First observation after starting the game is a simple "wow am I even playing Portal?".
It's much bigger game, has a lot more to tell, a lot more to experience. Snarky comments of our only proper AI - GLaDOS are just a chef's kiss. Wheatley presents less intelligent humour, however it's pretty entertaining. 
I guess the main question while creating Portal 2 was "how to immerse people better so they wouldn't feel it's a cheap copy?" and let me tell you - it is executed really well.
There is a ton of new mechanics, you get a proper storyline, you get fun coop experience and even community chambers which you can play if you already finished everything and you're starved for more.
Although I still wish that riddles would be harder. I felt it's a little bit too easy.

Achievements could be perfection if not for the Professor Portal one - I get it, we try to promote our game, find someone new to teach how to play Portal! It's a b*llshit of an achievement. As much as hugging three people is awesome - hugging your premade and some friends, teaching someone new to play is just an unfair marketing tactic, which now is difficult to be done, a LOT OF PEOPLE already played this game. 

Summarising, Portal 2 is how sequels should be done. Not using the reputation to earn money - GIVING an experience to your players, giving them what they want. This is probably why after this many years this game is still worth playing - it's made to be good. And it is good.

Portal 2 is a great game, but I think it tries too hard in some places. How many characters and plots do we really need to have for a physics puzzle platformer with a silent protagonist? Portal 1 gives you some peace and quiet to think through your options and make a plan. In the sequel it seems there's always some annoying racket going on in the facility while you're trying to think, or somebody is expositing some dialogue that, to its credit, is often quite humorous, but usually only ever "quite". Yes, Wheatley is entertaining. Cave Johnson is probably the best. GLaDOS is just... kind of annoying? Yeah, some of her dialogue can be funny, but after tens of test chambers the whole "I don't like you" schtick wears off. She does get better towards the end.

That being said, there are a lot of new and fun mechanics added. Light bridges, all three gels, spring plates, tractor beams, lasers, and so on. Nothing to say; new mechanics are, of course, innovative, and they're used well here.

The game is certainly longer than its predecessor; about three times as much in terms of singleplayer content, and even more counting co-op and player made levels. This is of course a good thing. The increase in the SIZE of levels, however, can cause issues in just finding where you need to go in the first place. Portal 2 likes to use the "find the portal surface in this massive room" game and it can get old fast. To its credit, the game often makes it pretty clear where you need to go. But the times it doesn't can get a little frustrating. 

Overall it's still a good game, and I'd get it alongside Portal 1 on sale, but if I had to play only one of the two again I actually might rather play the original.

Portal 2 is a rare sequel that improves on its predecessor in nearly every way. Developed by Valve, the game combines brilliant puzzle design, exceptional writing, memorable characters, and polished gameplay into an experience that remains outstanding years after its release.

The core mechanic—using a portal gun to create linked portals and navigate increasingly complex test chambers—is easy to understand but allows for incredibly creative and challenging puzzles. Each new mechanic is introduced gradually, making the learning curve feel natural while constantly presenting fresh challenges. The puzzles are satisfying to solve because they reward logical thinking rather than trial and error.

The story is surprisingly engaging for a puzzle game. The interactions between GLaDOS and Wheatley provide some of the funniest and most memorable dialogue in gaming. The writing is clever, witty, and consistently entertaining, making even transitions between puzzle sections enjoyable.

Visually, the game still holds up remarkably well. The environments of Aperture Science Enrichment Center feel distinct and atmospheric, ranging from pristine testing chambers to fascinating abandoned sections that reveal the facility's history. The sound design and voice acting are equally impressive and contribute greatly to the game's immersive atmosphere.

Another major strength is the cooperative mode, which offers a completely separate campaign with unique puzzles designed specifically for two players. It encourages teamwork and communication while maintaining the same high standard of puzzle design found in the single-player experience.

Few games manage to balance challenge, humor, storytelling, and innovation as effectively as Portal 2. Whether you're a fan of puzzle games or simply looking for a memorable gaming experience, Portal 2 is an absolute must-play and remains one of the finest video games ever created.

This is one of those rare games where almost everything just works. The puzzles are smart without feeling unfair, the writing is sharp, and the whole thing has that Valve confidence where it teaches you complicated ideas so smoothly you don’t notice you’re being trained like a lab rat with slightly better shoes.

The humor is a huge part of why it’s so memorable. GLaDOS is still perfect, Wheatley is a disaster in the best way, and Cave Johnson sounds like a man who could turn terrible business decisions into company policy with full confidence. The game is funny without stopping every five seconds to beg you to laugh, which is harder than it sounds.

I also love how the puzzles keep adding new layers. Portals, lasers, gels, light bridges, momentum, timing — it all builds naturally, and when you finally solve a room, you feel clever for about three seconds before realizing the game probably planned that feeling too.

And then there’s co-op, which is basically a friendship test with portals. Great idea, questionable communication, both players blaming physics. Perfect.

Still one of the best puzzle games ever made. Smart, funny, clean, creative, and somehow still fresh years later.

Portal 2 to me is the absolute pinnacle of what a modern video game should strive to be. Everything about it is fine tuned to be as enjoyable an experience as possible, and a big part of that is because the game can be beat in only a day or two. This largely linear self-contained experience is exactly as long as it needs to be, and does overstay its welcome. As a result, you get an experience that is an absolute blast from start to finish. No long grindey periods that feel pointless, no annoying padding, nothing. The game's absolute lack of bloat in any significant fashion plays a huge part into what makes this game as incredible as it is.

The game's largely realistic but also stylized graphics are also timeless and still look stunning today (the lack of visible human characters aside from occasionally seeing Chell through portals also helps, since human characters age the worst in realistic looking games). The music matches the mood perfectly. The story is interesting and engaging without overtaking the gameplay in any meaningful way.

What if you took a game, a game that was already really good, and made a sequel of said game by making it like 10 times better? Whatever example you may have in your head, throw it out the window and revel in the beauty of the sequel to the first Portal, Portal 2. If the first Portal is a unique experience, then Portal 2 is a drug designed to stimulate you out the wazoo and boy howdy does it deliver. The callback to the first game, the references to the world around you (y'know, the other Valve titles), and the sheer amount of lore and insults thrown your way is commendable. In the first Portal, it's a game that was clearly designed in an earlier era of gaming, by an up and coming studio that was testing some real cool stuff. Portal 2 is the result of letting developers work their magic and understand more about what it is the players want in a game, and more importantly, a Portal game. Portal 2 delivers far more content than the first title, be it by simply giving you more puzzles to work with, or by going around the Aperture Science facility (instead of being trapped in the fairly sterile rooms like in the first game). Not to mention, a ton more voice acting and interaction with the AI that make you feel less like a test subject and more like an escapee. It may not be a long game, but there's also the multiplayer action that can supplement a ton more hours with friends, and quite a bit of support within the modding community. All in all, it's a lovely game that I do believe everyone with the hardware should try.
